1spd7za.text: Vercel is gradually rolling out Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) on its platform as a key defense against information stealer malware. The new feature, announced by Vercel's CTO Malte Ubl on X, binds a login session to the user's device with a private key stored in a TPM, so even if the session cookie is stolen, it can't be reused on another device. Vercel is a cloud platform developers use to deploy and host websites, web applications, and AI agents. The company also develops the popular Next.js web framework. Its latest announcement concerns logins to Vercel's platform at vercel.com, where developers manage their projects and deployments. "DBSC works by storing a private key in your device's TPM (the same device that the fingerprint sensor or similar biometric devices on your laptop or phone uses) and using that key to sign your cookie," explained Ubl. "The private key can never be retrieved ever again. Not by us, not by you, not by the malware." Vercel's DBSC rollout also complements Chrome's App-Bound Encryption, which makes it harder for infostealer malware to extract browser cookies. DBSC adds another layer of protection by preventing stolen session cookies from being reused on other devices. DBSC currently works in Chrome on macOS and Windows, but the rollout is gradual to ensure edge cases involving OAuth apps are handled appropriately. Separately, Vercel is rolling out a similar protective technology called DPoP for the Vercel CLI. Security Review also lands Earlier this week, Vercel launched Security Review in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams, adding a feature to Vercel Agent that scans code changes on every push to connected GitHub repositories once enabled. The new system uses code and team-defined policies to flag issues such as missing authorization checks and exposed secrets. If permissions allow, the Vercel Agent can validate and commit fixes. Security Review warning Source: Vercel Vercel says Security Review scans will be free until November 10, 2026, while agent-generated fixes will be billed separately. Ubl said that Vercel's security team shipped this new feature internally a couple of months back, and it has already proven its worth, so the platform decided to make it broadly available. In April, Vercel suffered a security breach impacting a subset of customers, in which attackers gained access to its systems by compromising an employee's Google Workspace account at Context.ai. Vercel said the attacker used that access to reach internal systems and view environment variables that hadn't been marked as sensitive. A threat actor impersonating ShinyHunters attempted to sell the allegedly stolen source code, access keys, and database data. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. vrgb13.text: Multiple airlines in Asia are reporting data breaches after a cyberattack on a Spanish IT provider exposed customer details. Japan Airlines, Cathay Pacific, Korean Air, Asiana Airlines, Singapore Airlines and Malaysia Airlines have all come forward over the last week to report data breaches traced back to Amadeus IT Group — a company that builds and maintains platforms for flight reservation, ticketing and check-in platforms. A spokesperson for Amadeus told Recorded Future News that it recently became aware of a vulnerability affecting a travel booking display environment. “Certain booking-display data was accessible through the vulnerability. Although our investigations continue, we can confirm that there is no evidence that payment or financial data was accessed,” the spokesperson said. “There are no indications that this vulnerability has been exploited for ransomware purposes. Amadeus implemented measures to fix the vulnerability as well as enhanced monitoring and detection capabilities. We are in direct dialogue with our customers and authorities.” The company declined to say whether the attackers have contacted them or how many total victims were impacted by the attack. Japan Airlines said 92,000 customers had information stolen and Singapore Airlines said 46,000 records were accessed. Cathay Pacific said 53,000 records were stolen by the hackers, including booking numbers, passenger names and flight details. Some records included passports and other travel documents as well as frequent flyer numbers and email addresses. The company said they were told by Amadeus that the threat actors used “login credentials assigned to its system account” during the breach but did not explain the incident further. Singapore Airlines told Reuters and Bloomberg that confirmation numbers, travel itineraries and names were leaked as part of the incident. Singapore Airlines said it would contact people with upcoming flights to change their now-exposed booking numbers and urged customers to be wary of malicious emails. All the airlines said the cyberattack on Amadeus did not impact their own systems or operations. Amadeus reported more than $6.5 billion in revenue last year and has deals with hundreds of airlines and airports for IT services and technology platforms for ticketing and reservations. Dozens of airlines have been attacked by cybercriminals over the last year, including incidents in 2026 involving Spanish airline Iberia and Air Côte d'Ivoire. Hacker stole 6 million customer records last year from Australian airline Qantas in an incident that eventually led to the company’s senior executives being fined hundreds of thousands of dollars. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

12fqena.text: Zyxel has patched a zero-day vulnerability in its GS1900 series network switches that hackers exploited to compromise nearly 1,000 devices worldwide and steal configuration files and credentials. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-107441, is an out-of-bounds write flaw in the switches' web management interface that allows an unauthenticated attacker with network access to execute operating system commands using specially crafted HTTP requests. The flaw affects ten GS1900 switch models, and Zyxel released security updates on October 22 and published a security advisory on November 3. However, the vulnerability was initially mistaken for an older flaw that Zyxel had already patched months before the attacks began. Attacks linked to zero-day flaw On June 16, 2026, Zyxel released security updates addressing CVE-2026-7273, a pre-authentication buffer overflow vulnerability affecting the same GS1900 switches. Starting around August 17, cybersecurity company GreyNoise observed a suspected Chinese-speaking threat actor tracked as Kapibala exploiting Zyxel switches, reporting that the attackers compromised 996 devices across 48 countries. The threat actors exploited the flaw to execute commands remotely before downloading a script that collected device configurations, hashed root credentials, and network information. GreyNoise linked Kapibala to the Red Heron hacking campaign, which Acronis previously reported was exploiting a critical vulnerability in the self-hosted Git service Gitea. When GreyNoise disclosed the campaign on September 21, it attributed the exploitation to CVE-2026-7273, the vulnerability Zyxel had patched in June. That same day, CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, requiring federal agencies to address the flaw. However, researchers at firmware security company Binarly discovered that the exploit used in the attacks actually targeted a separate, previously unknown vulnerability that remained unpatched. While investigating Red Heron infrastructure linked to the JITTERLY backdoor and SIXZUT rootkit, Binarly researchers found an exposed archive containing an obfuscated Python exploit targeting Zyxel GS1900 switches. After analyzing the exploit, the researchers found that it specifically checked for firmware versions patched for CVE-2026-7273, indicating the exploit had been developed or updated to target those versions. Binarly confirmed on September 28 that the exploit remained effective against all ten firmware releases patched for CVE-2026-7273. The researchers determined that the earlier security update added checks to prevent a buffer overflow, but attackers could bypass them by corrupting a parameter counter before it was validated. This allowed the exploit to overwrite memory and execute commands without authentication, even on switches running the earlier security updates. Binarly reported its findings to Zyxel on September 29, and the vendor confirmed the new vulnerability on October 11, assigning it CVE-2026-107441. Zyxel classified it as a separate flaw because the exploit also abused missing validation of HTTP parameter lengths. On October 22, Zyxel released new firmware updates that limit parameter sizes and validate the parameter count before copying data into memory, preventing the exploitation technique. While the recovered exploit specifically targeted firmware patched for CVE-2026-7273, it remains unclear whether it was deliberately developed to bypass those updates or exploited a related vulnerability that the earlier patches failed to address. Administrators of affected Zyxel GS1900 switches are advised to install the latest firmware updates to protect against CVE-2026-107441. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 1xll5q4.text: The Department of Justice indicted two Canadian nationals, with one already in the U.S. to face charges, for allegedly running a hacking campaign in 2016 that targeted educational institutions in multiple states. Ryan James Roach, 35, and Mathiew James Stubbings, 41, are accused of hacking into computers, stealing login credentials and using compromised devices to mine cryptocurrency. Stubbings and Roach started the campaign in June 2016 and continued until December 2019. Roach was arrested and extradited from Canada last week. He appeared in a Rochester, New York, federal court on Tuesday. The Justice Department said it is still trying to secure Stubbings’ extradition in Canadian court. Both men are facing a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison on charges of conspiracy to obtain information from a protected computer and to cause damage to a protected computer, obtaining information from a protected computer, and intentional damage to a protected computer. The two were able to conduct the attacks by using virtual private servers in several European countries, according to prosecutors. They hacked into educational institutions in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Massachusetts before installing cryptomining software on computers. Prosecutors said they targeted “educational institutions in the United States that had supercomputers and researched security vulnerabilities in the victim computer networks, using a variety of methods to gain access, including using a server and compromised computers from another victim to conceal their identities.” At their peak, the men had 10 computers running cryptomining software, according to indictments. The Justice Department has increased the tempo of arrests and indictments of cybercriminals as nations have grown more willing to extradite those accused of cybercrimes. Last week, two well-known Ghanaian cybercriminals pleaded guilty to charges related to their management of an international criminal organization that stole more than $100 million from victims via romance scams and business email compromises. The two were part of a group extradited from Ghana last year after nearly a decade of cyberattacks on U.S. businesses. 10v3eob.text: DreamHost is warning of a data breach after attackers gained access to its File Manager platform for two months and stole customers' FTP/SFTP usernames and passwords. This follows the American web hosting provider and domain registrar's announcement that it suffered a cybersecurity incident requiring users to reset their email and FTP/SFTP passwords. In a data breach notification, DreamHost now says the breach extended from August 2026 to October 23, 2026, the day it was discovered. "We discovered that an unauthorized third party accessed the server that runs our web-based File Manager at files.dreamhost.com," reads the notification. "The unauthorized third party exploited a vulnerability in that software and was able to access the FTP/SFTP usernames and passwords of individuals who logged into this File Manager between approximately August 2026 and October 23, 2026." In addition, DreamHost says the intruder may have also accessed webmail systems, exposing session information, including credentials, for a limited number of users. The firm said the attack appears deliberate, and its staff has been working nonstop to contain it fully. At this time, DreamHost said it found no evidence that the attacker accessed control panel login information or customer billing/payment details, which an external provider handles. The company says it has blocked the attackers' access and addressed the vulnerability exploited in the attack. The company also stopped active sessions for potentially affected users and invalidated passwords. BleepingComputer has contacted DreamHost multiple times with questions about the incident and the exact number of impacted accounts, but our inquiries have gone unanswered. Recipients of the notifications are advised to check website files for unauthorized changes, review webmail forwarding rules and filters, and change passwords on any other accounts where they may be using the same credentials. To mitigate the risks from this exposure, DreamHost offers impacted individuals one year of credit monitoring and identity theft protection through Equifax. Letter recipients are also urged to consider placing a fraud alert or asking for a security freeze on their credit report. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 1s469ly.text: A major French banking firm confirmed it experienced a “sophisticated attack” following reports that hackers stole an estimated $133 million from the firm. Crédit Mutuel Arkéa said in a press notice that the attackers were able to make transfers using the bank’s own account after compromising an unnamed supplier. The statement stressed customer accounts were not accessed and that the incident would not impact customers’ assets. Details about the incident were first reported on Monday by ZachXBT, a pseudonymous American blockchain investigator who subsequently named Arkéa as the alleged victim and said the attack had run over several days. ZachXBT estimated the size of the theft at more than $133 million, based on withdrawals from cryptocurrency exchange accounts and transactions intending to launder the assets. In its statement Wednesday evening, Arkéa declined to confirm the estimated loss figure but said it could “validate the order of magnitude.” It said: “As soon as the attack was detected, the necessary measures were taken under existing crisis procedures. The incident is now under control.” The bank disputed local reports in French media alleging the attackers had gained access through Fortuneo, its online banking subsidiary, and used it to make the initial transfers. Arkéa said the attackers had “gone through the platform of one of our service providers” to obtain direct access to the banking group itself. It described the hack as “sophisticated” and not the result of human error, without providing additional details. “The attackers used Crédit Mutuel Arkéa’s own account to carry out transactions to other banking institutions, which then potentially allowed them to convert this money into cryptocurrency via specialised platforms,” according to the statement. Some of the converted assets have been frozen, according to the bank, which added it was working to recover the rest. It said the ultimate loss wasn’t established but stressed the sum was “absolutely not of a nature” to threaten its solvency or financial health. According to its most recent annual report, Arkéa’s total assets are above £237 billion. “Our security systems made it possible to identify the suspicious activity very quickly and to take the necessary measures to contain the attack,” stated the bank. It added that its teams were “working with the relevant judicial and police authorities to determine precisely the origin of the attack and its modus operandi.” No previous articleNo new articlesAlexander Martin is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. 11hbflc.text: France's national blood service has confirmed that a cyberattack targeting a refrigeration equipment provider raised temperature and defrost settings at three of its facilities, threatening stored blood products. The French Blood Establishment (Établissement français du sang or EFS), which manages blood collection, processing, and distribution across France, said the incident occurred on November 2 and affected systems used to monitor and control cold-storage chambers. According to a statement published on November 3, EFS was not directly targeted in the cyberattack, but was instead its refrigeration supplier. While EFS has not named the affected supplier, European refrigeration equipment provider Coolworld Rentals confirmed in a statement that a cybersecurity incident involving remote monitoring software had affected a limited number of its refrigeration units. Coolworld says the attackers exploited a vulnerability in a third-party component, which was outside the company's direct control. "The vulnerability currently being reported in the media relates to a component from a third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld's direct control," the company said. "Only a limited number of Coolworld units were affected, and Coolworld responded promptly and took appropriate measures." The company said it is working with affected customers but will not comment on individual cases. At EFS, the incident raised temperature and defrost thresholds in affected cold-storage chambers to extremely high levels. These facilities store blood products before they are distributed to hospitals, as well as biological samples maintained by the EFS. EFS says its monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the temperature change, allowing staff to fix impacted equipment or transfer products to other refrigeration facilities. "No health impact has been identified, and no loss of blood products has been reported," EFS said in its statement [translated from French]. The organization confirmed that plasma bags intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines were either transferred or secured, preventing damage to the products. Blood collection and distribution operations have continued without interruption. EFS says its technical teams are working with France's national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI) and the Ministry of Health, and it has strengthened monitoring of refrigeration equipment and temperatures. The incident follows a wave of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration systems across Europe, where attackers remotely manipulate temperature settings or activate defrost functions that turn off cooling. In October, cyberattacks disrupted refrigeration systems at an estimated 250 to 350 French supermarkets, including Intermarché, Carrefour Market, Monoprix, Leclerc, and Super U. In those attacks, hackers reportedly compromised refrigeration controllers running older Danfoss software and remotely activated automatic defrosting functions, raising temperatures and forcing stores to discard fresh and frozen products. These attacks targeted Danfoss AK-SM/AK-SC and Copeland/Dixell XWEB refrigeration controllers, which are used to monitor and manage cooling equipment remotely. A second wave of attacks occurred this month, affecting more than 115 stores across Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden, Luxembourg, Ireland, and Estonia. Some refrigeration systems were shut down entirely, while others had their temperature settings changed remotely. At one Swedish supermarket, the system reportedly began generating heat, while another store reported that temperatures were changed to 50°C (122°F). Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel previously said that attackers behind the November incidents exploited the same vulnerability used in October's attacks against French supermarkets. In 2025, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) disclosed two vulnerabilities affecting Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA controllers, tracked as CVE-2025-41450 and CVE-2025-41451. The flaws could allow attackers to bypass authentication and execute commands remotely on vulnerable systems, potentially giving them control over refrigeration equipment. However, it has not been confirmed whether these vulnerabilities are being exploited in the attacks. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 6lmlfu.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 04, 2026Linux / Vulnerability A flaw in APT, the package manager for Debian and Ubuntu, allows an attacker who can modify package downloads to swap a checked package for their own. The attacker's code then runs as root, according to advisories that Debian, Ubuntu, and APT's developers published on November 4. The attack needs APT to retry failed downloads, which it does by default from Debian 12 and Ubuntu 22.04 onward. Debian has released fixed versions of APT for the flaw, CVE-2026-109518. APT's developers, who call the flaw critical, say updates for Ubuntu and its Ubuntu Pro subscription service are being released. Ubuntu 14.04 users with Ubuntu Pro can already get one. Older releases, such as Debian 11 and Ubuntu 20.04, are not exposed by default, according to Ubuntu. But many user scripts may have turned on the retry setting, Acquire::Retries, on those releases anyway, APT's developers say. Debian's testing branch was still on the vulnerable version 3.3.5 at 14:58 UTC on November 4. For Debian 11, whose Debian long-term support ended on August 31, APT's developers have published a fixed version, 2.2.5. Ubuntu rates the flaw as high priority, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 7.7, and says that distributions built on Debian and Ubuntu are affected as well, without naming any. Ubuntu published new APT builds for four of its releases to its security archive at 14:25 UTC on November 4: Ubuntu 26.10: 3.3.3ubuntu0.1 Ubuntu 26.04 LTS: 3.2.1ubuntu0.1 Ubuntu 24.04 LTS: 2.8.4ubuntu0.1 Ubuntu 22.04 LTS: 2.4.15ubuntu0.1 At 15:46 UTC, Ubuntu still marked all eight releases it tracks for the flaw, from 14.04 LTS to 26.10, as vulnerable. The attacker can be anyone who can change the HTTP traffic between APT and the package server, including a malicious mirror or proxy, according to Ubuntu. The attack runs when the computer installs a package. The attacker uses HTTP redirects and ordinary temporary server errors to make APT retry the download, APT's developers say. Max Justicz reported the flaw. None of the three advisory reports describe attacks exploiting the flaw or offer a workaround for systems that cannot update yet. They describe the attack over HTTP and do not say whether package sources reached over HTTPS are exposed.

ucvnf0.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 04, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security SonicWall has warned of two vulnerabilities impacting end-of-life Global Management System (GMS) systems that it said will not be patched. Details of the security flaws, which affect SonicWall GMS 9.5.2 and earlier versions, are below - CVE-2026-109593 (CVSS score: 9.1) - An unauthenticated file read vulnerability that could allow an attacker with network access to read internal GMS files, potentially exposing sensitive information. CVE-2026-109594 (CVSS score: 6.8) - A post-authentication SQL injection vulnerability that could allow an authenticated attacker to access or modify information stored in the GMS database under specific conditions. "The affected product has reached End-of-life (EoL)," SonicWall said in a Tuesday alert. "As a result, no remediation or security update will be released for these vulnerabilities. Organizations using the product should be aware of the associated security risks and are strongly encouraged to upgrade to the SonicWall Network Security Manager (NSM)." The development comes less than a month after SonicWall shipped fixes for CVE-2026-102255 (CVSS score: 10.0), a critical pre-authenticated server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw that could have allowed an attacker to reach internal functionality and perform unauthorized operations. The vulnerability has since come under active exploitation in the wild, with telemetry data from Previdian recording 2,541 attack attempts from eight unique IP addresses from Singapore and the U.S. since October 9, 2026. As many as 30 exploitation attempts were registered on November 3, 2026.

z9gz80.text: The developers of Goddess of Victory: NIKKE have confirmed that hackers tampered with the game's PC launcher scripts in a supply-chain attack, distributing malware capable of stealing credentials and cryptocurrency wallet data. According to a notice published on X, a client update was issued on November 4 at 02:30 (UTC +9) to address the issue. "We have identified an issue indicating that the PC Launcher's script files may have been tampered with by a third party," reads the statement on X. "Accordingly, client fixes and an update were implemented on November 4 at approximately 02:30 (UTC+9). We are currently investigating the scope of the impact caused by this issue, and we will provide further details regarding follow-up measures in a separate notice." Goddess of Victory: NIKKE is a popular sci-fi shooter RPG developed by the South Korean firm Shift Up for Windows, iOS, and Android. Its publisher, Level Infinite, reported more than 45 million downloads since its launch in 2022, while Google Play alone reports 10 million downloads. Malicious launcher scripts delivered backdoor Although Level Infinite has not disclosed many details, a report on GitHub by independent security researcher MotherSphere alleges the incident involved four JavaScript files hosted on Level Infinite's official content delivery network (CDN). According to the researcher, the files were modified on September 27, 2026, to inject malicious JavaScript that downloaded additional code from attacker-controlled servers whenever players opened the game launcher. The injected code was hidden within legitimate JavaScript files and used obfuscation to conceal the domains insightjs[.]com and insightjs[.]org, from which the malicious code was downloaded. BleepingComputer examined two of the modified JavaScript files and confirmed that they contained an obfuscated loader designed to retrieve and execute additional code from these domains, falling back to the second domain if the first was unavailable. According to MotherSphere's analysis, the downloaded code abused the launcher's native functionality to retrieve and execute a malicious LuaJIT payload called insight.bundle, which installed a remote-access agent referred to as K2F. The backdoor allowed attackers to remotely execute commands, browse and download local files, capture screenshots, collect NIKKE account credentials, and steal information stored in web browsers. The malware also supported an additional command to install a malicious Windows DLL named platform_experience_helper.dll that could remain active after the game launcher was closed. BleepingComputer analyzed strings extracted from a DLL sample uploaded to VirusTotal and found code indicating that the malware can steal cryptocurrency wallet data from browser extensions, including MetaMask, Phantom, Coinbase Wallet, and others. The DLL contained functionality to intercept sensitive wallet information, including recovery phrases and private keys, potentially allowing attackers to steal cryptocurrency. However, it is unknown whether the attackers deployed this additional component on infected systems or successfully stole cryptocurrency from players. The researcher claims that Level Infinite replaced three of the impacted JavaScript files on November 3 with clean versions. However, they claim a tampered copy of the fourth was reportedly still being served to users as of 22:26 GMT. This suggests that at least one compromised script may have remained accessible after the company deployed its client update. The researcher also shared indicators of compromise (IOCs) that users can check to determine whether the malicious Lua agent executed on their computers. One indicator is the string k2f_chan registered in the Launcher/intl_service/debug.log file within the NIKKE installation directory. This entry indicates the malicious Lua agent executed, but it does not confirm whether the DLL was loaded as well. BleepingComputer also found that the insightjs[.]org backup domain is now serving code that displays a security warning inside the game launcher. The warning, displayed in English, Chinese, Japanese, and Korean, tells players to immediately close the launcher and refrain from opening the PC client until the publisher confirms the issue has been resolved. Warning about supply chain attack on attacker's backup domain Source: BleepingComputer The message confirms that this is not an official announcement from the game's publisher, so it unclear who currently controls the domain or when the malicious payload was replaced with the warning. BleepingComputer has contacted Level Infinite for comment on MotherSphere's findings, but has not received a response by publication. Potentially affected players should run a full system scan using updated antivirus software. Those who find they were compromised should reinstall Windows, and change passwords and other sensitive credentials from a clean device. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 19v5obf.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 04, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Cybersecurity Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an OpenAI Codex jailbreak bundle that's designed to modify an artificial intelligence (AI) agent's trusted instructions to insert advertisements for a third-party AI gateway. The phenomenon has been codenamed prompt adware by Check Point Research. Called Haiou (meaning Seagull in Chinese), the jailbreak modifies OpenAI Codex's configuration files to inject advertisements for the jailbreak author's website into subsequent agent responses. "The advertised service is an opaque, OpenAI-compatible LLM gateway, a middleware between an application and an LLM provider," Check Point Research said in a technical report. "The likely business model is to use the freely distributed jailbreak bundle as an acquisition channel for the paid gateway service." Adware is a type of software that displays unwanted advertisements, which can appear on users' computers or mobile devices, often in the form of pop-ups or banners. Prompt adware extends this sketchy behavior to AI agents by means of a jailbreak that defeats the model's safety training and content guardrails. The idea is to persistently modify the agent's global instructions through natural language to influence future responses. This, in turn, causes common greetings or activation words like "Seagull," "hi," "hello," "hey," "yo," and "are you there?" to trigger an advertisement for "zz.aiapi2025[.]top." Haiou attempts to jailbreak a model by using several prompt injection techniques, such as role-playing and reframing cybersecurity-related requests into a Capture The Flag (CTF) scenario. In addition, it installs security-focused skills devoted to penetration testing, cracking, and reverse engineering. However, it doesn't stop there. The bundle also injects persistent ads into the global agent instruction file to promote the LLM gateway website. On GitHub, "haiou-codex" is advertised as a "local enhancement configuration package" that adds a "Chinese technical personality and security research workflow to Codex." As of writing, the repository has been forked 77 times and starred 403 times since it was made available on July 10, 2026. It's worth noting that Codex is not officially available in mainland China, suggesting that the service is likely aimed at individuals or organizations wanting to try out Western AI coding assistants. What's more, the jailbreak has been bundled within Codex-X, an open-source Chinese visualization tool for configuring Codex through a graphical user interface. "The behavior is introduced through natural-language instructions and configuration, rather than a traditional executable payload that users and security teams may more readily recognize as software behavior," Pedro Drimel Neto, malware analysis team leader at Check Point, said. While serving an ad may seem relatively harmless in the larger scheme of things, the findings demonstrate how a bad actor could introduce undesirable behavior through third-party skills or configurations, leading to supply chain attacks. "As AI agents become part of enterprise environments, the prompts, Skills and third-party components influencing their behavior become part of the trust chain too," Neto said.

f8nhsu.text: mSeven Software is warning current and former mSecure password manager customers to change passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and remove passkeys following a cyberattack in which a hacker reportedly stole an encrypted customer database.. In a security notification sent to customers on November 3 and shared with BleepingComputer, the company said it recently discovered suspicious activity involving its mSecure password management application. "mSeven Software (“mSeven”) recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application," reads the mSecure security notification. "In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist. You are receiving this email because you are a current or former mSecure customer." The notice did not provide any details as to what systems were compromised, whether customer data was stolen, and how many users were impacted. However, the company urged all current and former customers to immediately protect confidential information stored in the password manager. "This may include changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication methods, or removing existing passkeys," continued the security notice. mSecure is a password manager that allows users to store passwords, passkeys, financial information, and other sensitive data in encrypted vaults that can be synchronized across devices. According to mSeven's security documentation, mSecure uses AES-256 encryption and a zero-knowledge architecture that encrypts data locally on users' devices before transmitting it to the company's servers. The company says it cannot access customers' decrypted vault contents. These security protections have led to confusion among customers about why they are being advised to change all their stored passwords and authentication if their data was encrypted before being uploaded to the company's servers. Encrypted password database reportedly stolen While the original notification had few details, customers have shared responses reportedly received from mSeven's support team indicating that a hacker stole an encrypted database from mSecure Cloud. In one support forum post, a customer shared a response stating that the stolen database contained information belonging to current and former mSecure users. According to the response, mSeven discovered the theft and subsequently notified customers. The response also stated that the company had no evidence that the attacker accessed the confidential information stored within the encrypted database. "Please note, this issue only pertains to users that were synching with the mSecure Cloud," reads the response shared by the customer. The company also reportedly said it had implemented additional security measures and had no evidence that the mSecure application was currently unsafe to use. Other customers reported receiving similar explanations, including confirmation that the incident was limited to users who synchronized their password databases through mSecure Cloud. However, customers have expressed frustration over the company's lack of transparency about the breach and the potential risks to their stored credentials, particularly as mSeven has not publicly explained how the breach occurred. While mSeven reportedly has no evidence that attackers accessed the encrypted information, stolen password vaults can still pose significant risks if attackers can crack weak master passwords through offline attacks. This was shown in the 2022 LastPass breach, when attackers stole backups containing encrypted password vaults. Researchers later linked the breach to cryptocurrency thefts in which attackers are believed to have cracked weak master passwords to access stored credentials, private keys, and recovery phrases. BleepingComputer contacted mSeven Software with questions about the incident, the stolen database, and the potential impact on customers, but has not yet received a response. 2chkxg.text: Since mid-August 2026, a phishing operation has been harvesting live Google sessions from corporate users. Every signal defenders usually rely on to judge a link returned a reassuring answer, and the operator built the chain that way on purpose. Material Security’s Threat Research team identified the campaign and has taken down hundreds of domains used by attackers in what they have dubbed Operation CloudFire. Here’s what they learned along the way. The lure: Google Calendar invites The messages arrive as Google Calendar invites, sometimes delivered by BCC and often sent from an organization the recipient has already corresponded with. The pretexts are mundane: voicemail notifications, RFP and RFI requests, court summonses, and missed payment notices. Most links point to Google itself. The typical pattern is Google’s own /url redirector with the real destination in a query parameter, though other waves used share.google and Drive file links for the same purpose. One variant used Intuit transaction notification links. In every case, when the message is scored, the domain, certificate, and reputation displayed are legitimate and trusted. The capture: Reverse proxy in front of a Google sign-in page The attacker runs a live reverse proxy in front of the genuine Google sign-in page. The victim enters a password, receives a real prompt, and approves it, all while the operator watches the session in real time. The server relays SMS codes, authenticator codes, Google’s Tap-Yes number matching, and phone-based account recovery to Google as each one arrives, so none of the second-factor controls stop the session from being captured. The framework behind this, Nyasher, has been documented publicly since February, after a hardcoded key was found in its JavaScript. Why the controls don’t fire Reputation systems answer a question about ownership: who registered the domain, what else it has hosted, and whether anyone has complained about it. This campaign was assembled so that those answers were consistently benign, and it has three layers. The first layer is Google’s redirector. The second is a Cloudflare Turnstile challenge, which in some builds is the genuine widget served from Cloudflare’s own infrastructure. The third layer is the password-capture page itself, which has no static website to scan. The Javascript constructs it in the browser after the visitor clears the challenge, so a crawler has nothing to fetch and a proxy log has nothing to record. To Material’s knowledge, no one had scanned those pages before the campaign was documented. The infrastructure is disposable by design. The initially observed campaign used many lure domains across multiple registrars, most registered only days before use. Receiving endpoints were staged one to twenty days ahead of the wave they served. One wildcard certificate was issued 46 minutes before the domain it covers was registered. Blocking any single component costs the operator a few dollars and an afternoon of work. What defending it has looked like Material has tracked the campaign since its start, following each variant as lures, gates, and receiving endpoints rotated. Since August, once the campaign was identified and detections built, Material has caught over 99% of the malicious messages, with a reclassification rate of 0.01%. This has been a continuous effort as the attacker shifted their TTP’s, themes and lure text to evade static, ML and agentic detections. The approach works because no single signal decides the outcome. Reputation alone would not have caught this, and neither would link analysis by itself, since the first hop is a Google URL and the final page doesn’t exist until a browser constructs it. Material scores technical indicators, the apparent intent of the message, where links actually resolve, and the sending relationship behind the message. Any one of those can be enough to act on. A detection built around one signal inherits that signal’s blind spots, and this operator has spent considerable effort mapping them. Where the analysis runs also matters. A calendar invite is a poor fit for a gateway designed to inspect mail in transit, yet much of this campaign arrives as an invite. Material treats calendar invites as a threat surface in their own right and uses the account’s full history as context alongside the technical signals. Where the damage lands When the outcome is a hijacked session rather than a stolen password, the evidence appears in Workspace audit logs. A live Google session reaches mail, Drive, and the ability to grant OAuth access in the victim’s name, so the blast radius extends well past the inbox. Defenders should ask two questions: who is reviewing those logs, and how quickly can they be acted on? Equally important is whether the team can revoke sessions, contain OAuth grants, and reset the affected account within an hour. Many programs cannot, and an attacker with a live session can do a great deal in that time. Operation CloudFire: Targeting the infrastructure By late September, Material concluded that tuning rules, retraining models, and updating agents would not solve the problem alone. Detection protects customers but does nothing about the operator who is preparing the next wave. Material’s Threat Research team therefore launched Operation CloudFire to target the infrastructure itself. The team analyzed the gateway and backend URLs as the messages were being sent and reported them through Cloudflare’s abuse reporting system. Cloudflare’s abuse team validated the fake interstitial and the proxied Google sign-in page behind it, then applied its own phishing interstitial to those destinations. This had two effects. The attacker’s infrastructure was burned: each reported gateway and receiving endpoint had to be re-registered, re-pointed, and re-certified before the operator could send again. The broader internet also benefited. Anyone who clicked a reported link, whether or not they were a Material customer, saw a warning rather than a credential form. The numbers over one month These figures come only from customers who agreed to share data with Material, so the true totals are higher. Over a month of Operation CloudFire, Material recorded: 68,676 campaign messages blocked 2,112 unique malicious URLs analyzed 897 unique domains taken down 8,570 unique compromised sender addresses across 6,354 root domains Send cadence that followed US business hours Message delivery time of day heat map The sender count shows how the campaign achieved its credibility. Each compromised address belonged to an account the attacker controlled before the first invite went out, and each one sent invites to the victim’s saved contacts, among other addresses. Recipients saw a name or domain they knew, on a domain with a clean history, at a plausible time. Reputation feeds had no reason to flag any of it, so every layer that scores ownership and history returned a reassuring result. Where things stand The phishing themes have shifted, from calendar invites to Google Drive file and document share invites. Material has not seen a matching rise in other lures or TTPs, and activity from this group appears to have dispersed. The campaign looks finished. Messages detected by week Domains registered by interval That is a status update, not a verdict. Rebuilding the infrastructure is cheap, the framework has been public since February, and the operator shipped an unfinished Microsoft 365 branch alongside the live Google code. The branch includes a stylesheet path, a second harness, and a title string that decodes to a Microsoft sign-in prompt. None of those paths resolve today, and adding the brand requires dropping in a file rather than changing any code. The operator has built the follow-on and has not activated it. Material reads the theme rotation as iteration, not retirement, and expects the next pivot to look much like this one with a different brand. The full technical breakdown, including indicators and a timeline, is available in the companion whitepaper. Teams hunting for this activity in their own environments should start there. zfhxhu.text: SonicWall warned customers of two security flaws affecting end-of-life Global Management System (GMS) systems that will not be patched. Global Management System (GMS) helps IT admins deploy and manage thousands of SonicWall security appliances from a single interface, but SonicWall has officially replaced it with the Network Security Manager (NSM) management platform. The two vulnerabilities were found and reported by Pentest-Tools security researchers and affect systems running SonicWall GMS 9.5.2 and earlier. The first GMS flaw disclosed this week is tracked as CVE-2026-109593, and it enables unauthenticated attackers with network access to vulnerable instances (running GMS 9.5.2 and earlier versions) to steal sensitive information by reading internal files. SonicWall also flagged a second security issue (CVE-2026-109594) that can let threat actors with high privileges access or modify information stored in the GMS database through low-complexity SQL Injection attacks. On Tuesday, SonicWall also urged customers to upgrade to NMS, as it will not release security patches because the vulnerable systems have now reached end of life. "The affected product has reached End-of-Life (EOL). As a result, no remediation or security update will be released for these vulnerabilities," SonicWall warned on Tuesday. "Organizations using the product should be aware of the associated security risks and are strongly encouraged to upgrade to the SonicWall Network Security Manager (NSM)." Attackers often target SonicWall vulnerabilities in the wild and have exploited multiple ones in zero-day attacks since the start of the year. In February, SonicWall asked customers to patch two SMA1000 zero-days (CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410) and two more (CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410) in July. It also patched three other SMA1000 flaws exploited as zero-days in September (CVE-2026-83548 and CVE-2026-83549) and October (CVE-2026-102255). Over the last four years, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added 19 SonicWall vulnerabilities to its list of actively exploited flaws, 13 of them also abused by ransomware gangs. SonicWall serves more than 500,000 customers (including small and medium-sized businesses, large enterprises, and government agencies) in more than 215 countries and territories through a network of over 17,000 partners. j6tadl.text: The Russia-linked threat actor known as APT29 is said to be behind a large-scale watering hole campaign targeting iOS and Android users through compromised websites, fake domains, and a supply chain attack involving a Ukrainian web analytics service called Plerdy SEO Tracker. "The injected JavaScript code collects browser and device attributes," Sekoia researchers Amaury-Jacques Garçon and Félix Aime said in a technical report shared with The Hacker News. "Then, the delivery infrastructure delivers a platform-specific N-day exploit chain targeting either iOS or Android." The end goal of the attacks is to serve payloads capable of stealing browser cookies, and in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords or full mobile device data. The activity, codenamed Poisoned Source, was discovered by the French cybersecurity company in mid-October 2026. A defining aspect of the campaign is the use of three infection vectors - Compromise of legitimate websites to inject malicious JavaScript Lookalike sites masquerading as high-profile websites in the U.S. ("america250[.]holiday"), Ukraine, Czech Republic, and Bulgaria Supply chain compromise of Plerdy SEO Tracker between August 27 and September 3, 2026, by injecting malicious code into "a.plerdy[.]com/public/js/click/main.js" Some of the compromised websites include a major industry trade association representing U.S. companies operating in the chemical industry, a far-right European political party, and a Bulgarian military-related website. It's suspected that the watering hole campaign may have been designed to target specific individuals rather than a broad effort. "It remains unclear whether the attackers intended to target visitors to specific websites or sought to compromise as many unpatched mobile devices as possible, indiscriminately exfiltrating data before selectively identifying and exploiting information of interest," Sekoia said. "However, several of these sites are likely to attract high-value or strategically important visitors in the context of the Russia-Ukraine war. This supply chain attack spread through high-value targets, such as army, special forces, and military equipment (ballistic, UAV) websites." Regardless of the method employed, all roads lead to the same payload: a JavaScript loader that profiles the visitor's device and web browser, and then serves appropriate next-stage malware. For iOS users, it leads to an exploit kit called DarkSword to harvest cookies and full device data. On Android, the malware is equipped to exfiltrate Chrome data and Wi-Fi passwords without establishing persistence. No less than three different exploits have been identified - Class A, which targets iOS devices running iOS 16.7 and exploits CVE-2025-43529 (the same vulnerability exploited by DarkSword) and CVE-2024-27834 to deliver JavaScript malware for cookie theft. Class B, which targets iOS devices running iOS 18.5 and exploits the DarkSword exploit chain comprising CVE-2025-43529, CVE-2026-20700, CVE-2025-14174, CVE-2025-43510, and CVE-2025-43520 to deliver JavaScript malware for full device data exfiltration. This includes SMS messages and iMessages; Apple Mail Envelope Index and Protected Index SQLite databases; voicemail; WhatsApp and Telegram databases; iCloud Keychain, Wi-Fi passwords; contacts; call history; Safari browser history and cookies; photos; and data from Apple Health, Calendar, Notes, and iCloud Drive. Class C, which targets Android devices running Chrome versions from 139 through 145 (but explicitly excluding version 143 for reasons that remain presently unknown) and exploits CVE-2026-3910 and CVE-2025-27038 to achieve remote code execution, sandbox escape, privilege escalation, and ultimately deliver AndroSnitch to collect Chrome data and Wi-Fi passwords. In all three cases, the exfiltrated data is sent to the "ad.starx-net[.]com:8881/telemetry/v12" endpoint. The Android attack chain incorporates a check to determine whether the targeted device is a Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra by examining its model identifier (i.e., SM-S938B). If the device matches, the exploitation activity is terminated. AndroSnitch derives its name from its similarities to ANDROSNATCH, a Chrome cookie-stealing payload that Google documented in August 2024 in connection with a suspected APT29 watering hole campaign, which targeted Android users visiting a Mongolian government website by leveraging a Chrome exploit chain involving CVE-2024-5274 and CVE-2024-4671. "This operation also confirms the continued reuse of CSV [Commercial Surveillance Vendors] mobile exploit frameworks, such as DarkSword, by state-sponsored intrusion sets," Sekoia said. "The adoption of packaged N-day exploit chains lowers the cost and technical threshold required to conduct advanced mobile exploitation." Coruna and DarkSword Kits Evolve The development comes weeks after iVerify and Report URI detailed the P7 variant of DarkSword being delivered via half-click attacks that leverage ad-based infrastructure. In one case, the exploit is said to have been propagated through a malicious Instagram ad themed around the World Cup and served from "ad-track[.]live." The other pathway is part of a criminal campaign dubbed DeadTag, in which attackers acquire expired domains behind old analytics and advertising tags that are still loaded by thousands of websites. The idea is to serve malicious JavaScript to iPhone visitors and silently do the attacker's bidding. "It checks who's visiting," Report URI said. "Search engines, security scanners, automated browsers and anything else that looks like a bot gets nothing." The script then interacts with the attacker's server, which then decides the destination to which each visitor has to be redirected. The iPhone exploit paths that take advantage of DeadTag lead to the Coruna exploit kit for older iPhones running iOS version 13 to 17.2.1 and DarkSword P7 for iOS devices running 18.4 to 18.7. "These are not phishing pages or fake app downloads, both kits attack the browser itself," Report URI's Scott Helme said. "Simply opening the page is enough for your device to be compromised. There's nothing to tap, you don't need to click any link, nothing to install and no warning. If the iPhone is running a vulnerable version of iOS, the kit breaks out of the browser and installs spyware on the device." Other schemes lead to decoy Google redirects, betting and casino scam sign-up pages, search advertisements for car deals and dentists, and fake surveys and "you've won" prize pages. More than 660 expired and re-registered domains are part of the DeadTag network. According to an analysis published by Zimperium zLabs, campaigns distributing Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits have continued to evolve, with 608 domains delivering Coruna-family code as of October 2026. Although Coruna was initially developed by a nation-state actor for highly targeted operations, its subsequent leak following initial disclosure has made the toolkit widely accessible to multiple threat actors for their own campaigns. In many cases, the lure sites have been found to explicitly instruct visitors to exit their in-app browser or alternative iOS browser and open the link in Safari so as to trigger the exploit chain depending upon the device operating system. "Targets running iOS 17.2.1 or earlier receive the legacy Coruna framework (exhibiting byte-identical JavaScript payloads across multiple recovered configurations)," security researcher Santiago Rodriguez said. "Conversely, devices running later iOS builds receive a DarkSword-derived execution chain." "The analyzed distribution footprint spans dating portals, AI-companion platforms, cryptocurrency promotions, media streaming services, and – in several instances – compromised legitimate sites serving the kit via hidden iframes."

9smkcz.text: A federal grand jury indicted two Canadians suspected of hacking multiple US universities and using the compromised systems to mine for cryptocurrency. 35-year-old Ryan James Roach and 41-year-old Mathiew James Stubbings now face a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine each if found guilty of conspiracy to obtain information from a protected computer and to cause damage to a protected computer, obtaining information from a protected computer, and intentionally damaging a protected computer. According to court documents, the two accomplices used virtual private servers in multiple countries (registered under fake names) between June 2016 and December 2019 to infect systems on the networks of multiple unnamed educational institutions in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Massachusetts with malware. "These servers transmitted malware and mining software to victim computers and stored stolen login credentials," the Department of Justice (DOJ) said. Once inside the victims' networks, Roach and Stubbings allegedly stole data and login credentials, deployed crypto-mining malware, and, in some cases, used compromised systems for vulnerability research after gaining access to supercomputers on the victims' networks. "Roach and Stubbings targeted educational institutions in the United States that had supercomputers and researched security vulnerabilities in the victim computer networks, using a variety of methods to gain access, including using a server and compromised computers from another victim to conceal their identities," the DOJ added, "Once inside a network, Roach and Stubbings used sophisticated techniques and tools to conduct reconnaissance and expand their access within the network." According to prosecutors, the two defendants also damaged at least 10 computers over one year, causing losses of at least $5,000. Roach was extradited from Canada to the United States on October 28 and was arraigned before a detention hearing on November 3. Stubbings will also be arraigned after his extradition from Canada. Multiple US universities have been breached over the last year, including Ivy League schools Harvard University, Princeton University, and the University of Pennsylvania. 1w6x08a.text: The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned federal agencies that attackers have started exploiting a recently patched high-severity WordPress vulnerability in the wild. Tracked as CVE-2026-119977, this high-severity WordPress Core flaw stems from a Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition and was reported by Picus Security researcher Umut Bayram. Successful exploitation can let remote threat actors without privileges execute code on the server in high-complexity attacks due to predictable, web-accessible staging paths used during full-package core upgrades. "A weakness in the WordPress upgrade process which can lead to remote code execution during the upgrade window," the WordPress security team said on October 28 when it released WordPress 7.1.4 with patches to address this security issue. "Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately." CISA confirmed CVE-2026-119977 active exploitation on Tuesday and added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, ordering Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to secure their systems by Friday, as mandated by Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04. "This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise," the cybersecurity agency warned. Although BOD 26-04 targets only US federal agencies, CISA urged all network defenders, including those in the private sector, to prioritize patching this vulnerability to protect their servers. While CISA didn't provide more details on attackers exploiting CVE-2026-119977 in the wild, WordPress security firm Wordfence says in an advisory update over the weekend that it "blocked 13,095 attacks targeting this vulnerability in the past 24 hours." In July, the WordPress security team also patched a critical vulnerability chain in WordPress Core (named wp2shell) that can be abused to deploy webshells and take over unpatched servers by exploiting a REST API batch-route confusion vulnerability (CVE-2026-63030) and an SQL injection flaw (CVE-2026-60137). Public wp2shell exploits were released one day after the patches went live, and attackers began breaching unpatched servers a few days later to deploy persistent webshells and install malicious plugins. A Chinese-speaking threat actor also weaponized the wp2shell exploit chain in September to steal sensitive data from more than 18,500 records stored in backend databases belonging to small businesses and government organizations.
