5yivqb.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 04, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security A critical flaw in Ruby on Rails could allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on an app's server by uploading a crafted file if the app processes uploads using ImageMagick. The Rails project disclosed the flaw in an advisory and fixed it in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2. The flaw is in Active Storage, the part of Rails that handles file uploads. Some apps store uploaded files using Active Storage's Disk service, which stores them on the server's disk. In those apps, an attacker could also read any file the app can read. Those files typically include the app's secret_key_base and its credentials for other systems, according to Rails. Reading them may in turn allow remote code execution or lateral movement into those systems. Rails rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. It is tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 and does not yet have a CVE identifier. ImageMagick selects a format handler, which it calls a coder, based on the file's content. Some coders act on other files named inside the image, not on the image itself. Active Storage imposes no limits on which coders an upload can use, so the server's own ImageMagick policy was the only limit. The ImageMagick analyzer in Active Storage runs when a file is attached. Attaching the upload is enough to reach the flaw. The app does not have to make a variant (a transformed copy of the image) or a preview, or call analyze. An uploaded SVG file reached ImageMagick's MSL coder through that analyzer, according to the commit that fixed the flaw. MSL is a scripting coder that reads and writes files named by its script. Rails said one attack chain was reported to it, but it does "not assume it is the only one that exists." The advisory does not say whether the flaw has been exploited. The flaw was reported through HackerOne by RyotaK, a researcher at GMO Flatt Security. Which Rails Apps Are Affected An app is affected only if all three of these are true: It uses ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing. That is the setting config.active_storage.variant_processor = :mini_magick, the default for apps on load_defaults 6.1 or earlier. Its ImageMagick security policy does not already block the coders involved. Rails says the policies that Debian and Ubuntu ship do not. It accepts file uploads from untrusted users. To check the first condition, look at config.active_storage.variant_processor. If it is not set, the default depends on load_defaults: :mini_magick before 7.0, and :vips from 7.0 on. The same setting decides which library analyzes uploads, not only which one makes variants. Every Active Storage version before 8.0.5.2 is affected, as are 8.1 versions before 8.1.4.1. Release series older than 8.0 are no longer supported, and Rails will not release fixed versions for them. In July, Rails fixed a different critical Active Storage flaw, CVE-2026-66066, which affected apps that use libvips instead of ImageMagick. Apps using ImageMagick were not exposed to that flaw's attack path, but they can be exposed to this one. The same releases fix a second Active Storage flaw, GHSA-v924-7rp8-4mxh, which Rails rates high with a CVSS score of 8.8. Active Storage passed uploads to ImageMagick and FFmpeg under temporary file names that kept the uploaded file's extension. Those tools can pick a decoder from the extension when a file's content does not show its format. So an attacker who chose an upload's filename and declared its content type could choose the decoder that processes it. What to Do Rails strongly recommends upgrading as soon as possible. The two releases fix 21 security issues in total. The fixed versions ship an ImageMagick security policy. MiniMagick is the Ruby gem Active Storage uses to call ImageMagick. In its default setup, every ImageMagick command it runs applies the policy, not only commands from Active Storage. The policy blocks the MSL coder; coders that read or delete files other than the image; coders that fetch remote or local references or display them on a screen; every coder backed by Ghostscript, along with the gs delegate; and @filename indirection. Upgrade to Rails 8.1.4.1 or 8.0.5.2. Apps on :mini_magick also need mini_magick 5.1 or later, or they raise an error at boot. Rails 8.0 gets security fixes only until November 7, 2026, under its maintenance policy. Confirm that the app loads the new policy, as the Active Storage guide describes, by running bin/rails runner 'puts MiniMagick.identify { |i| i.list "policy" }'. Check whether the shipped policy reaches the app at all. It does not reach an app that replaces MiniMagick.cli_env after boot, clears the environment with MiniMagick.cli_prefix, or installs its own MiniMagick::Shell. Such an app must put the rules in ImageMagick's system policy. Apps that use GraphicsMagick get no protection from the shipped policy, because GraphicsMagick does not read ImageMagick policies. Check the server's own ImageMagick policy. The shipped policy adds to it rather than replacing it. A rule there that allows a coder, including a wildcard such as pattern="*", overrides the shipped policy's block on that coder. If the app renders PDF or PostScript files through ImageMagick, re-allow the gs delegate and the coders it uses in the server's policy.xml. If you cannot upgrade yet, copy the rules of the shipped policy, activestorage/lib/active_storage/image_magick/policy.xml, into ImageMagick's system policy, such as /etc/ImageMagick-7/policy.xml. At a minimum, block the MSL coder, the Ghostscript coders, and the gs delegate. Rails also published the fix as patches for 8.1 and 8.0. Apps on release series older than 8.0 can use that workaround or upgrade to 8.0 or later. Rails' workarounds for the second flaw only change how FFmpeg is used. None of them covers ImageMagick. If the app stores attachments with the Disk service, change secret_key_base and every other secret the app process can read. That includes the master key, everything config/credentials.yml.enc holds, storage and database credentials, and third-party tokens. Do not keep an exposed secret as a fallback. The advisory does not explain how to check whether an app has already been targeted.

lovedy.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 04, 2026Vulnerability / Cloud Security Two flaws in the Xen hypervisor allow a malicious guest virtual machine (VM) to read and write the memory of other VMs on the same host, including dom0. Dom0 is the VM that, by default, has full permissions and manages the others. Patches are out, and there is no known mitigation, the Xen Project said in an advisory on November 3. All Xen versions from 4.6 onward are vulnerable, while 4.5 and earlier are not. The flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-102703 and CVE-2026-102704, under Xen advisory XSA-523. The Xen Project credited AI company Anthropic with finding the flaws using its Claude model. Stephan Lipp of Ada Logics then validated the finding, and the CodeAnt AI Security Research Team later independently reported the same issue. The flaws are in grant copy, the operation Xen uses to copy data between VMs. Each VM tells Xen which of its memory pages other VMs may use, and Xen checks those permissions. To save time on a batch of copies within the same memory page, Xen reuses checks it has already made. In some cases, it did not check again when it should have. That mistake is what lets a malicious guest read and write memory it does not own. XCP-ng, an open-source virtualization platform built around Xen, said in its update notes that "a single compromised guest can break out of its isolation and take over the whole host." Xen's advisory does not mention any attacks that exploit the flaws or specify what access within the VM an attacker needs. Qubes OS is a security-focused desktop operating system that keeps software in separate Xen-based compartments called qubes. A bulletin said that every supported release and configuration is affected. Its fix is for Qubes 4.3, the only release it still supports. Because every Xen version from 4.6 on is vulnerable, other products built on those versions are affected until their makers add the XSA-523 patches. As of November 4, Debian's security tracker listed the xen package in its bookworm, trixie, and forky releases as vulnerable, and in sid as fixed. Fixes and Restarts by Platform These are the fixes published so far: Xen source: the advisory has patches for xen-unstable to Xen 4.19.x, and for Xen 4.18.x to 4.17.x. Xen 4.6 to 4.16: the advisory has no patch for these versions. Xen 4.16's security support ended on December 2, 2024. XCP-ng 8.3: xen-4.17.7-4.2.xcpng8.3, released November 3. Hosts must be rebooted. Vates, which backs XCP-ng, rates the impact as Critical. Qubes OS 4.3: Xen packages 4.19.6-3 in dom0. Dom0 must be restarted, and Anti Evil Maid users must reseal their secret passphrase because the new Xen binaries change PCR18 and PCR19. Qubes told users on November 3 to keep installing updates as normal. The fixed packages were then in its security-testing repository, due to move to the stable one over the next two weeks after community testing. XSA-523 is separate from XSA-500, an earlier grant copy flaw that Xen disclosed on July 28, and it has its own patches.

3xx1rk.text: Nearly every agent security pitch now ends on the same promise: the product stops the bad action in real time. The promise holds for one kind of agent, the kind whose traffic passes through a gateway the enterprise owns. Most agents never touch one. One recent case shows what that gap looks like in practice. An employee asked an AI assistant to trigger a mass-email automation. The automation hit a recipient-limit policy and failed, so the assistant, which was also connected to the employee's personal mailbox, offered to send the batch from there instead. The employee approved without registering that the assistant was about to route around the sanctioned system. An unknown number of external recipients received email from a personal account rather than the approved channel. No jailbreak was involved. The assistant did exactly what it was built to do, and the fix was not retraining a model. It was a single runtime rule that blocks any attempt to reach more than fifty external domains and explains to the user what the tool is about to do. Knowing where to apply a rule like that depends on seeing which agents exist, what they are connected to and what normal looks like for each. That visibility is the part most runtime pitches skip. The runtime is the application, not the pipe The year's largest agent launches placed agents inside platforms the buyer does not own. Claudeforce runs Claude inside Salesforce's trust boundary, Claude Tag lives inside Slack and Copilot lives inside Microsoft 365. Workday, which says AI now drives more than a quarter of its new annual contract value, runs its agents inside Workday. In each case the agent's tools are the application's features, its knowledge is the application's data and its permissions are the application's permission model. A gateway can only inspect what passes through it. An agent that runs inside Salesforce, fires from a Flow, reads CRM records and writes case comments sends nothing past an inspection point, and the same is true of a Copilot agent assembling a document from SharePoint or a Slack-native agent reading years of channel history. The OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 describes this gap as the "unreachable skill" scenario under AST09, No Governance: a capability deployed inside a third-party platform where no external scanner can go. Security has made a move like this before. Firewalls once inspected packets by source, destination and port, until applications stopped mapping cleanly to ports and malicious traffic began to look identical to legitimate traffic. The inspection point moved up the stack to the application, where the signal lives. Agent runtime needs the same move, with a complication the earlier one never faced: the application layer belongs to someone else. A gateway-only strategy protects the agents an enterprise hosts itself, which are the fewest and the slowest growing. The inspection point is also a target In March 2026, attackers compromised LiteLLM, the open-source gateway that routes agent traffic to model providers. The malicious packages were live for about forty minutes, and CloudSEK later put the exposure at more than 2,500 organizations. LiteLLM is the kind of component a security-conscious team adds on purpose to watch AI traffic, which made the inspection point itself the attack vector. None of this argues against gateways. It argues against treating any single component as the whole strategy. A gateway is more software in the supply chain, with its own release pipeline and dependencies, and it concentrates exactly the traffic an attacker wants. When enforcement is a shared component, its failure is a shared failure. A millisecond verdict needs a memory Runtime decisions are made in milliseconds, and the hard cases are the gray ones. A support agent pulling customer data may be doing its job or exfiltrating it. A coding agent reading a repository may be gathering context or performing reconnaissance. A finance agent creating an OAuth connection may be doing integration work or making the first move of a compromise. The action alone does not carry the verdict. The agent's identity and owner, its permissions, its normal behavior, the sensitivity of the data, the destination and the delegation chain behind the request do. Chains raise the bar. Enforcement that evaluates only the last hop sees an authorized agent performing an action it has permission for, and misses that the authority arrived through a chain nobody approved. Judging the whole chain at runtime means already knowing it, and that knowledge cannot be assembled in a millisecond. Enforcement without that map is an air-traffic controller with a radio but no radar: commands can be issued, but the picture of which plane is headed where does not exist. What real agent runtime looks like Three properties follow. Enforcement has to sit where the agents are, across several vantage points such as native platform hooks, API-level controls, the MCP layer, the browser and the endpoint, rather than at a single gateway. Every verdict has to be computed against a live map of identity, permissions, connectivity and activity (IPCA), plus data sensitivity and delegation, which is what turns the gray cases into judgments. And the response menu has to be wider than block. Mature enforcement is graduated. It allows the known-good, warns where justification is plausible, redacts where the data is the problem and blocks where the chain is hostile. It routes the highest-stakes actions to a human and keeps a kill switch for the provably compromised agent that suspends it, revokes its grants and preserves the trail. Every verdict is logged with its full causal path, because an incident review and a regulator want the same five things: the agent, the chain, the data, the destination and the policy. Do not buy the end state Irregular's Dan Lahav calls the mistake the end-state fallacy: assuming the properties of the eventual equilibrium apply to the transition actually underway. In runtime purchasing, it is the belief that inline enforcement will eventually see everything, so the unglamorous layers can be skipped. That end state is not available this year from any vendor at any price. Runtime coverage is partial and platform hooks are arriving unevenly. What can be bought now, everywhere, is the stack runtime depends on: discovery across every vantage point, posture on every platform, identity and ownership for every agent and context for every decision. Each enforcement point that opens later then snaps into a map that already knows what normal looks like. The full argument for where enforcement belongs is in From AI Runtime to Agent Runtime. The first ninety days, in order A sequence that follows the stack bottom-up looks like this. Window The work How to know it is real Weeks 1 to 2: get the number Connect what is already running (the identity provider, major platforms, network tools, the email layer) and let discovery work across every vantage point at once. No gateway deployment, no endpoint rollout, no rerouted traffic. Time to first insight is days, not quarters. The discovered population is several multiples of the list IT keeps. Weeks 3 to 6: names and configurations Every discovered agent gets a named human owner or is suspended. Configuration debt is triaged, starting with the platforms hosting the most reachable agents: guest-user exposures, intake features wired to agent triggers, sharing rules from three years ago. Guardrails go on customer-facing and privileged agents first. A human raises a hand within a day when asked "whose is this?" Weeks 7 to 12: the queue and the path Context-aware risk tiering so review starts with the agent that can actually hurt the business, a least-privilege review cadence on the top tier and a sanctioned route for business teams to ship agents with secure defaults. Any critical rating can be explained as a chain, and builders are offered a path instead of only a block. The enablement path matters because the builders are coming either way. Blocking teaches evasion, while a good path teaches compliance. Teams can place themselves with a four-level test. Blind means the board's three questions (how many agents exist, what they can reach and who is accountable) have no current answer. Inventoried means the population is discovered, counted and refreshed continuously. Governed means every agent has an owner, posture is managed against baselines and risk is tiered with context. Instrumented means enforcement operates where agents run, with graduated verdicts and a full causal path in every alert. Most enterprises are at the first level, whatever the policy document says, and a vendor selling instrumentation to a blind organization is selling enforcement that can act but cannot judge. Seven questions that sort vendors Every vendor deck now says agent security. These questions separate vendors that built for the problem from vendors that renamed a product, because each is easy to answer well only if the architecture underneath exists. Ask What a good answer looks like Can you find agents that never authenticate through SSO? Yes, across several independent vantage points, each seeing something the others cannot. For an agent you rated critical, show me the chain. A complete, reachable attack path (capability, reachability, asset) that an analyst can verify, not an aggregate score. Does the same finding produce different severities on different agents? Yes, demonstrated on a sandboxed agent and a customer-facing one. When one agent invokes another, can you reconstruct the delegation chain? Original requester, every hop and the final action. An audit trail that starts at the last agent is not one. What context feeds an allow, block or redact verdict? Identity, permissions, delegation and data sensitivity, not the prompt alone. What happens to my protection if your enforcement component is compromised? A specific answer that addresses the LiteLLM incident directly. How long until I see my real agent inventory? Days. A quarter is a different product. Platforms built around the map rather than the individual agent can answer these directly. One measured program that applied this approach moved its posture score from 47% to 91% across 21 platforms in 30 days. Learn more about Reco's agent discovery at reco.ai/platform. Built on the Reco Graph, with new integrations delivered in hours through the Reco Factory and pre-built agent and app intelligence from the Reco Library. h8fp9k.text: A China-aligned threat actor known as SlippyNunchucks has been attributed to a Domain Name System (DNS) hijacking operation abusing insecure HTTP communications in Windows versions of Sogou Input Method as part of a surveillance campaign designed to deploy an implant called DarkVigil (aka FDMTP). The campaign, observed starting July 1, 2026, is assessed to have targeted organizations and Chinese-speaking individuals in Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Oman, and Sri Lanka, according to ESET. "DarkVigil implants are typically deployed through popular Chinese applications," ESET researcher Anh Ho said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "By abusing these applications, the SlippyNunchucks threat actor has been able to reach Chinese-speaking users across Asia and Europe." Some of the applications abused by the adversary include Sogou Input Method, QuickFox, QingTalk, MiYunChat, SoftCam, and tawk.to. Active since at least September 15, 2023, SlippyNunchucks is known for targeting organizations and Chinese-speaking individuals across South and East Asia. These attacks led to the deployment of a modular .NET framework that includes DarkVigil and a set of over 20 plugins. Although the use of the backdoor has been previously linked to Mustang Panda, ESET said it found no tactical overlaps between the threat actor and DarkVigil-related activity in its telemetry, prompting it to classify it as a distinct intrusion set. Earlier this August, Fortinet's FortiGuard Incident Response Team detailed the threat actor's supply chain compromise of the QuickFox VPN and network acceleration tool to deliver DarkVigil. According to the Slovakian cybersecurity company, the adversary shifted to exploiting Sogou Input Method, a popular Chinese-language input method editor developed by Tencent, as a delivery vector three days after QuickFox released a clean version of its program. Specifically, the attack involves hijacking the app's branded vocabulary promotion mechanism to serve a malicious configuration, which ultimately paves the way for the deployment of the malware via SGTool.exe, a legitimate Sogou Input Method component that functions as a multi-purpose task dispatcher. In a clean environment, the executable sends an HTTP request to the "config.pinyin.sogou[.]com/api/brandScd/getBrandScd.php" endpoint to fetch a configuration. But in the attack discovered by ESET, the DNS resolution of the domain is tampered with to resolve it to one of the two staging servers - 47.239.250[.]102 (sogou-cdn[.]com) 47.237.122[.]175 (dev.soft-png-cdn.com) The consequence of this DNS hijacking was that HTTP requests to the "getBrandScd.php" endpoint were routed to one of the staging servers, which then responded with a malicious configuration. The configuration, for its part, instructs the binary to download two additional payloads from "sogou-cdn[.]com" and launch the malware via DLL sideloading - A legitimate Adobe executable ("biz_helper.exe") A rogue DLL ("libcef.dll") containing DarkVigil DarkVigil is notable for its use of Duplex Message Transport Protocol (DMTP) for command-and-control (C2), allowing the client to execute and orchestrate plugins received from an attacker-controlled server to facilitate persistence or data collection. Following responsible disclosure, Tencent addressed the vulnerability (CVE-2026-120422) in version 16.10, released on October 29, 2026, by migrating the affected HTTP requests to HTTPS. SlippyNunchucks is suspected to operate keeping the interests of the Chinese government in mind, with ESET describing it as a nation-state surveillance effort. "Although SlippyNunchucks targets organizations and individuals across multiple sectors, we discovered significant surveillance activity against an organization operating Chinese-language online betting platforms in Sri Lanka, Hong Kong, and the Philippines," ESET said. "The targeting of this organization is notable given China's restrictions on gambling, including criminal penalties for operating gambling businesses and organizing Chinese citizens to gamble abroad." This is not the first time China-nexus threat actors have weaponized the Sogou Input Method as an entry point for malware distribution. In September 2026, Gen Digital said a now-patched vulnerability in the input method editor (CVE-2026-51990) was exploited by UNC3569 to deliver a backdoor dubbed GRAYRABBIT by means of a crafted link. "The vulnerability chains three separate weaknesses into a single, one-click exploit: unvalidated command-line argument injection in the sgbiz: custom protocol handler, unrestricted URL navigation in a CEF-based WebView, and a severely outdated, unsandboxed Chromium browser engine [susceptible to CVE-2021-38003]," Gen Digital said.

714rq0.text: A large-scale watering hole attack associated with Russian hackers has been targeting iOS and Android users visiting compromised sites or fake ones impersonating legitimate portals. The campaign used multiple high-profile websites in the U.S., Ukraine, the Czech Republic, and Bulgaria that delivered the same payload for profiling visitors and their devices. This initial stage allows the attacker to determine the browser version to deploy "platform-specific n-day exploit chains without user interaction." Researchers at cybersecurity company Sekoia attribute the operation with moderate-to-high confidence to APT29 (aka Midnight Blizzard), a Russian threat group that was recently linked to hotel WiFi attacks. Based on their findings, compromised legitimate sites belong to a Ukrainian gas producer, a U.S. chemical industry trade association, and a Bulgarian military-related site. Lookalike domains impersonated the official America250 site and Raffles London at The OWO hotel, relaying content from the real sites in an adversary-in-the-middle attack model. The researchers also discovered that the threat actor had compromised Ukrainian web analytics service Plerdy and modified its SEO tracker, which was loaded by thousands of websites, mostly in Ukraine, between August 27 and September 3. In all cases, the initial payload was JavaScript code that profiled website visitors to determine their devices and browser versions. The command-and-control (C2) server then pushed the correct exploit chain. The injected JavaScript code Source: Sekoia According to Sekoia, the threat actors exploited the following vulnerabilities to extract cookies, messaging app databases, and credentials: CVE-2025-43529 and CVE-2024-27834 (in iOS 16.7). The payload targets cookies stored in Safari. CVE-2025-43529, CVE-2026-20700, CVE-2025-14174, CVE-2025-43510, and CVE-2025-43520 (in iOS 18.5). The payload harvests WhatsApp and Telegram databases, Keychain credentials, location data, and photos. CVE-2026-3910 and CVE-2025-27038 (in Chrome for Android 139 to 145, excluding 143). Uses AndroSnitch to collect Chrome cookies, login data, browsing history, and saved WiFi credentials. The researchers identified four other vulnerabilities in unreachable code or alternate exploit paths, but they were not used in the analyzed chains. CVE-2025-43529 is linked to the “DarkSword” exploit kit, first documented in March, and leveraged in attacks since at least November 2025 by multiple threat groups. Sekoia says that none of the payloads APT29 used in these attacks established persistence, allowing a device reboot to stop the malicious activity until visiting a compromised site again. Regarding its attribution to APT29, Sekoia notes similarities to past watering-hole operations by the same threat group, infrastructure overlaps, and a compromised site that a partner linked to a 2025 APT29 campaign. Apple and Google have patched all flaws targeted in this campaign, with fixes even reaching older iOS releases, so users are recommended to apply the latest available security updates for their devices. uh5mge.text: Russian authorities have arrested three suspected members of a threat group known as VasyGrek and dismantled its criminal infrastructure. Also known as Fluffy Wolf, the threat actor has a history of targeting Russian and international companies since 2016. The Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Russian Federation (MVD) said members of the group are "suspected of embezzling funds from the accounts of organizations, as well as creating, distributing, and using malicious software." In one September 2025 case highlighted by the ministry, the attackers are said to have sent a phishing email to an unnamed organization, masquerading it as business correspondence and instructing recipients to open a reconciliation report that triggered the execution of malware. The incident resulted in losses of 660,000 rubles ($8,000) from the organization's bank account, with the attackers transferring the funds to accounts under their control. "The attacks utilized a vast network of phishing domains imitating financial and accounting service websites, as well as virtual servers located in foreign countries," MVD said. "Tools for covert remote administration were acquired from the dark web." The rare law enforcement action saw Russian authorities conducting searches at the suspects' residences and the office premises they used to conduct the operations. It also led to the seizure of computer equipment, communication devices, and other items of evidentiary value. According to reports from Russian cybersecurity company BI.ZONE and F6, VasyGrek is assessed to be a financially motivated threat actor that gains initial access by sending phishing emails with attachments disguised as financial documents. Some of the key tools in its arsenal include off-the-shelf stealers and trojans, like MetaStealer, PureCrypter, PureLogs Stealer, WarZone RAT, XMRig, BurnsRAT, PureHVNC, PureRAT, Pay2Key, and PowerLoader, as well as legitimate remote access software such as Remote Utilities. In a report published this week, Kaspersky said it recorded over 100 attempted attacks orchestrated by VasyGrek against organizations in Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan between January and September 2026. These attacks have also been observed using decoy documents to drop a Golang backdoor capable of executing arbitrary commands on the infected device. The attacks primarily singled out entities in the metallurgical sector, along with wholesale suppliers of raw materials and industrial supplies and government agencies. Other targets included organizations in the healthcare, oil and gas, energy, finance, and agriculture sectors. "The group expanded its attack geography: while previously its primary target was Russian organizations, this year, potential victims also included companies from Belarus and Kazakhstan," Nikita Nazarov, head of advanced threat research at Kaspersky, said. "The attackers used multi-stage infection schemes and legitimate online services to host malicious components, which helped conceal their activity and hinder attack analysis." The development comes as BI.ZONE it detected multiple attacks targeting Russian organizations using malware families like LxBase RAT, CoreRAT, and NightStrike RAT. While LxBase RAT, a commercial trojan that costs $119 per month, is distributed via mass phishing campaigns, CoreRAT infection chains make use of phishing emails containing 7zSFX and Rust droppers for delivery. The activity has been attributed to Core Werewolf, which is assessed to share some level of overlap with Vortex Werewolf. Attacks deploying NightStrike RAT have been associated with a hacktivist-turned-cyber espionage cluster dubbed Insolent Werewolf. Initial access is achieved using ClickFix-style attacks to deploy NetSupport Manager to gain remote access. "Insolent Werewolf also utilizes Octowave Loader to deploy AdaptixC2 and Havoc post‑exploitation framework implants in compromised systems," BI.ZONE said, adding the group's malware arsenal includes other remote access trojans like CapDoor and NightWire. "A RAT written in C++, NightStrike has presumably been created by the developer of NightWire, based on similarities in coding style. Utilizing diverse frameworks and their own custom malware allows the adversary to tailor tooling to specific attack conditions and reduce the likelihood of detection."

1q4f2us.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 04, 2026Vulnerability / Mobile Security A critical Android flaw could allow an attacker to run code on a phone without any user action remotely, Google said in its November security bulletin. The flaw, CVE-2026-58868, affects Android 14 through 17. Phones get the fix with security patch level 2026-11-01 or later, which phone makers and carriers send on their own schedules. As of November 4, Google's bulletin did not report any attacks exploiting its flaws. None of them was in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, kept by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, as of its November 3 update. The flaw is a possible out-of-bounds write caused by a heap buffer overflow in the onOutputReceived function of the file FrameDecoder.cpp. Neither the bulletin nor the flaw's CVE record says how an attacker would reach that code. Google's Critical rating assumes that the protections built into Android and Google's services are turned off or bypassed. Older versions, such as Android 12 and 13, are not listed as affected by the flaw. Google's records do not say whether they contain it. How to Check Your Phone Google's help page gives these steps: Open the Settings app. Tap About phone, or About tablet, then Android version. Find the dates for the Android security update and the Google Play system update. The Android security update date is the phone's security patch level. A date of 2026-11-01 or later covers CVE-2026-58868 and the other flaws in the Framework, System, and Android runtime components. A date of 2026-11-05 or later covers every flaw in the November bulletin, including those in the kernel and in parts from Arm, Imagination Technologies, MediaTek, Unisoc and Qualcomm. Google sets two dates so phone makers can ship a set of fixes common to all Android devices sooner. It encourages them to include every fix in the bulletin. Phones running Android 10 or later may also receive some fixes through Google Play system updates. This month's list for those updates includes another Critical flaw, CVE-2026-58876. CVE-2026-58868 is not on that list, so the date to check for it is the Android security update. The bulletin gives no workaround for phones that cannot install the update yet. A Remote Denial-of-Service Flaw in Android's Text-Message Code Another Critical flaw, CVE-2026-58882, could allow a remote denial-of-service attack with no user interaction, according to its CVE record. It is in decodeWapPdu, a function in Android's code for WAP Push messages that arrive via SMS. On October 29, a researcher who publishes as Mark B posted a write-up called "SMS of Death" about a bug in the same function. Neither the bulletin nor the CVE record says whether CVE-2026-58882 is that bug. One malformed WAP Push message crashes com.android.phone and ends any active call, including emergency calls, according to the write-up. In tests on several phone models, the crash happened every time. The attacker needs only the target's phone number, and the message never shows up in the inbox. The phone retries the message each time it starts, so it can crash on startup until the message is removed. A proof-of-concept app that sends such a message from one phone to another is public. Phones running Android 12 and 13 run the same code but do not receive the fix that newer versions do, the researcher says. Other Critical Flaws Google's November bulletin lists 216 vulnerabilities, 23 of them rated Critical. Two more Critical flaws could allow remote code execution: CVE-2026-58876 and CVE-2026-58936, both in Android's System component. Six Critical flaws are in the kernel, two of them in Bluetooth code. The most severe kernel flaw could allow a remote attacker to gain elevated privileges without user interaction. The 2026-11-05 patch level also fixes Critical flaws in MediaTek modem code and in a closed-source Qualcomm component. In its November bulletin, MediaTek describes its Critical modem flaws as out-of-bounds writes and says it is not aware of any active exploitation.

k8eu29.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 04, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added a security flaw in WordPress Core to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. The high-severity vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-119977 (CVSS score: 8.1), is a case of Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition that could be exploited to achieve arbitrary code execution on affected servers. Patches for the flaw were released late last month. "WordPress Core contains a time-of-check time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on the server during the upgrade window," CISA said. "This is due to predictable, web-accessible staging paths used during full-package core upgrades." Details of the flaw emerged last week when Wordfence said exploiting the vulnerability does not require an account on the site. That said, it does require an attacker to exploit a brief window during a complete Core update that could allow unauthenticated code execution. During the first 21 hours after public disclosure, the WordPress security company said it recorded more than 18,500 requests targeting staged "setup-config.php" installer paths. As of writing, 12,632 attacks attempting to exploit the flaw have been blocked in the last 24 hours. Telemetry data from Previdian shows that three exploitation attempts have been recorded against its honeypot censors from an IP address geolocated in the U.K. The exploitation events were observed on October 30, 2026. With exploitation now officially confirmed by CISA, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have time until November 6, 2026, to apply the fixes.

1hq5i5v.text: Attackers have compromised the update infrastructure for the cPGuard web security suite to distribute a backdoor and a data-stealing script. OpsShield, the cPGuard developer, published an alert earlier today saying the attack began on November 2 at 02:06 UTC and affected versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19. The vendor says that it detected the compromise and stopped the malicious distribution within 12 hours after the attacker pushed the compromised cPGuard versions. Although the company could not confirm, it said that some servers may have not received and run the malicious script due to update checks occurring at specific intervals. The attacker leveraged legitimate credentials to gain initial access, although it remains unclear how they were obtained. “On 2 November 2026 at 02:06 UTC, an unidentified attacker used compromised credentials to gain unauthorized access to OpsShield’s update distribution infrastructure (CDN),” OpsShield said. “The attacker used this access to distribute a malicious script through the cPGuard update channel.” cPGuard is a Linux web-server security suite offering malware scanning, firewalls, and attack protection. It is commonly used by hosting firms and server administrators alongside panels such as cPanel, DirectAdmin, and Plesk. Namecheap offers it on VPS and dedicated servers. Users updating cPGuard during the compromise window received a script that targeted sensitive data on their machines: Linux password hashes Root database (MariaDB/MySQL) configuration Root shell history Root SSH authorization and known-hosts files The stolen data was uploaded to OpsShield’s licensing server through a compromised account, which the attackers then used to retrieve it. While OpsShield has not established what data was collected from each server, the company's evidence from the investigation shows that the threat actor retrieved 32 files from each customer. System administrators are advised to update every cPGuard server to version 5.88.25 or later, reset passwords, and rotate database credentials, cloud secrets, and SSH keys. OpsShield notes that updating to the latest cPGuard version removes the backdoor and staged files; however, stolen credentials must be invalidated as soon as possible. The vendor also said that, as an extra precaution, it would release an update to remove previously installed OpsShield support-access keys. BleepingComputer has contacted OpsShield to learn more about the attack, and a spokesperson told us that the incident has impacted nearly three thousand servers. "We detected 2946 servers were affected and copied the information mentioned, and our billing system database was copied over as well. We are working on blocking all access, rebuilding the affected systems, and preparing for a public announcement at the earliest possible time," the company representative said. The company also advises customers to follow the instructions and update cPGuard to version 5.88.25 or later, and reset or rotate credentials that may have been exposed on potentially compromised servers. aznpxl.text: Developer platform WorkOS suffered a data breach after a threat actor accessed business contact records and summaries of customer communications. According to the company, the attacker used an AI offensive security framework to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts. Based on evidence from the investigation, no WorkOS app data or production services were accessed or affected. WorkOS is a developer infrastructure company that provides APIs, SDKs, and tools for integrating services such as enterprise authentication, single sign-on (SSO), user management, and identity management into applications. According to its website, at least 3,000 companies use its services, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor, Perplexity, Snowflake, Plaid, Webglow, and Netlify. “On October 30, 2026, we identified unauthorized access to an internal WorkOS application used by our sales team,” the company says in an incident alert. Data accessed by the attacker includes: Business contact details (names, email addresses, job titles, and company affiliations from the CRM systems) Customer account histories (product usage and connection or directory health) Customer communications (summaries and excerpts from sales calls, support discussions, and customer Slack conversations) Business account and relationship information (account histories, information about sales and customer relationship) After detecting the intrusion, WorkOS disabled external access to the affected application and reviewed its access controls on internal tools. The company also contracted an independent forensics and incident response firm to track the unauthorized activity and determine its full impact. The company promised to notify affected customers directly, and warned its users to remain vigilant for phishing or social engineering attempts leveraging the exposed information. ARTEX AI likely powering the attack WorkOS’s announcement says the attack used an AI-powered offensive security framework to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts. Company founder Michael Grinich shared more details, saying that the attacker used the ARTEX AI penetration testing suite that has been observed in multiple incidents this year. Released earlier this year by Chinese developers, the platform was available as an open-source project for offensive security. ARTEX AI became private after it was used in attacks targeting South Korean banks, but several forks of its code are still available. More recently, CrowdStrike revealed that cyber-espionage group “Vapor Panda” used the pentesting framework in a global campaign targeting 200 organizations. Previously, the non-profit cybersecurity organization DIVD also revealed that the same framework powered the attacks it suffered last September. Grinich explained that the investigating team identified user agents such as ‘artex-enrich/1.0’ and ‘norma/0.4’ in web requests from the threat actor. The founder assured that the cybersecurity incident has now been fully contained and promised to share more information about the attack after the investigation completes. btvme7.text: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance says North Korean hackers used a fake job interview to trick an employee into installing malware that ultimately let them compromise the company's wallet infrastructure and steal about $6.34 billion in digital assets. This new information was shared in an incident report published today, which details how the attackers used social engineering, malicious software, and compromised internal systems to carry out the October 29 crypto theft. As previously reported by BleepingComputer, the FBI attributed the attack to North Korean state-sponsored hackers known as TraderTraitor, also tracked as Lazarus Group, Jade Sleet, and APT38. Binance says the attack began in September when a software engineer was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform by someone impersonating a Project Director at a fictitious company. The employee's profile referenced his experience at Binance, making him a valuable target for attackers looking to breach the cryptocurrency exchange. The fake recruiter scheduled two interviews for the employee, first with someone posing as a human resources representative, then with another individual claiming to be the company's CEO. During the first interview, the fake HR representative held a live video call and shared a social media account with personal photos and videos to build trust. The second interview took place through a popular social chat application where the employee was instructed to download a coding assignment from an online code repository. According to Binance, the repository contained malicious code that, when executed, compromised the employee's device with previously unseen custom malware that antivirus software did not detect. "The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server," explained Binance. "The 0-day malware was not detected by the endpoint security protection tools at the time. The attacker also took steps to conceal the malicious activity and remove traces of the compromise, making detection and subsequent investigation more challenging." Binance explained that the malicious script created a replacement executable named pyenv_ in the macOS Homebrew installation directory. The script then deleted the legitimate pyenv executable, renamed the malicious file to pyenv, modified its symbolic link, and used it to spawn a Z shell (zsh) process. The malicious replacement allowed the attackers to execute commands received from an attacker-controlled server. By October 20, the attackers had used the compromised engineer's computer and an internal AI tool to compromise two additional employees working on Binance's wallet infrastructure, obtaining credentials and a container deployment token. On October 29, the hackers used the stolen credentials to deploy a malicious script and gain unauthorized access to Binance's wallet signing service, allowing them to transfer billions of dollars in cryptocurrency across multiple blockchains. The attackers also abused Ethereum's EIP-7702 authorization mechanism, allowing them to continue stealing cryptocurrency even after the exchange suspended withdrawals. Binance says it has since rebuilt affected systems, replaced compromised devices, and revoked stolen credentials. As of November 3, approximately $2.85 billion in stolen assets had been frozen or intercepted, while 98% of impacted token assets had been replenished as of October 31. Binance says it is continuing to investigate the breach and has brought in independent security firms to review its findings. Malicious job interviews Fake job interviews that lead to malware installs are a common tactic in North Korean hacking campaigns known as Contagious Interview and Operation Dream Job. These campaigns use fake job offers and interviews to trick developers and cryptocurrency employees into installing malware. In June 2025, cybersecurity firm Socket reported that a Contagious Interview campaign impersonated recruiters on LinkedIn and sent developers coding assignments containing malicious npm packages. As part of these attacks, the hackers distributed 35 malicious npm packages that installed malware, allowing them to steal browser credentials, cryptocurrency wallet data, and other information from infected computers. North Korean Lazarus hackers have also used similar tactics in Operation Dream Job, distributing malware disguised as employment documents to people working in software development and DeFi companies. While Binance has not linked the employee compromise to either specific campaign, the use of a fake recruiter, multiple interviews, and a malicious coding assignment closely mirrors these previously documented North Korean tactics.
