k4wmho.text: A botnet of more than 1.3 million Android devices, mostly TV set-top boxes, lost control of its servers in late October in a takedown led by Google. Google says it is highly confident that device maker Videostrong intentionally put a backdoor in the boxes and sold access to criminals. They used the boxes for ad fraud and to pass other people's internet traffic through owners' home connections. The backdoor is still on the boxes, and owners cannot remove it themselves. Videostrong, based in Shenzhen, China, makes Android TV boxes and other devices under its own name and for other brands. The backdoor, called x.cpe, was built into many device models and brands over several years. Google does not believe a rogue insider or a mistake was to blame. Google used legal action to take down the domains and servers that controlled the botnet. It also took down the control domains of more than a dozen malware families loaded through the backdoor. Japan's National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient and TrendAI worked with Google on the operation. Because the criminals behind that malware also spread it in other ways, Google expects the action to cut off their access to at least 10 million more infected devices. It warns that backdoor operators and the criminals who buy from them quickly switch to new tools when one part of their setup is disrupted. Google has cut ties with Videostrong. It banned the company, and any future subsidiaries or affiliates, from building or selling certified Android devices and from supplying software to other certified device makers. What the Backdoor Did The x.cpe backdoor runs as a system app inside the firmware, with system-level access, according to Google's analysis. It reports to the botnet's command-and-control (C2) servers and waits for orders. To install software silently, it first turns off the app checks in Google Play Protect, Android's built-in security feature. Through the backdoor, the botnet's operators could install apps without the owner knowing, run commands, capture the screen and map the network the box sits on. Google says it saw Videostrong's operators use some of these powers. They took live screenshots, sent keystrokes, copied out account details, device information, app lists and system logs, and opened reverse shells, which give a remote command line into the box. Most of the criminals' modules, the add-on programs loaded through the backdoor, turned the boxes into residential proxies or sold their spare bandwidth. A residential proxy service sells access to a home internet connection, so a customer's traffic appears to come from an ordinary household. Other modules faked views of online ads. Most infected devices are Android TV set-top boxes, but the backdoor also turned up on telehealth devices, karaoke machines and digital signage. TrendAI, Trend Micro's enterprise business unit, counted 1,472,554 infected devices across 206 models between June 3 and October 1, and says the real number is at least that high. Malaysia, Brazil, Iraq, Mexico and Taiwan had the most. The U.S., Germany, the U.K., Australia and Canada each had about 26,000 to 42,000. What Owners Can Do Synthient, which tracks proxy networks and botnets, has published a list of 182 device model names seen in the campaign. The list warns that a model name alone does not confirm that a box is infected. Synthient's report focuses on MECOOL-branded boxes, which it links to Videostrong. It bought a MECOOL KM9PRO Max and found the backdoor preinstalled. Plume, which makes Wi-Fi software for internet providers, found more than a dozen different devices using the botnet's control server, most of them from MECOOL. Because x.cpe is part of the firmware, removing it does not stick. It reinstalls itself when the box restarts. TrendAI says the backdoor runs as a system app signed with the maker's key, so cleanup needs "vendor action, platform protection or replacement of the device." Plume recommends a full factory reset, because the modules may have installed more backdoors, but it does not say whether a reset removes x.cpe itself. Synthient goes further, telling consumers to throw the boxes away for good because they pose a high risk of malware. For organizations, Synthient recommends these steps: Use its published indicators to find MECOOL or similar devices on the network. Disconnect and throw away any that turn up. Block the control domains and IP addresses its report lists. Keep other smart devices on separate network segments, away from sensitive systems. TrendAI advises companies with remote staff to treat unmanaged consumer devices on home networks as part of their attack surface, and to keep corporate access behind managed devices. How Videostrong Was Identified In Google's account, x.cpe passes settings from the C2 server to other Videostrong apps, including its YokaTV Player streaming app. One of the GitHub accounts that hosted the botnet's packages is named yf-videostrong. Synthient, which worked with Google, also concluded with high confidence that Videostrong runs the operation. It points to a document signed by Videostrong's research and development director in an open folder on one of the botnet's servers, and to a Videostrong web domain that shares an IP address with the operators' control panel. Plume found that Videostrong supplies both the firmware for these devices and tools to manage them remotely. A Gap in Google's Device Tests Google requires device makers to go through a set of compatibility and security tests. It says Videostrong hid its code to bypass a gap in those tests and loaded the malicious code after a device's first boot. Google has changed its review process and is improving its checks of the firmware on certified Android TV devices. As of November 2, Videostrong's own website listed products it calls "Google Certified Android TV Box" and "Google Certified Android TV Stick." Plume says the botnet included both Google-certified devices and devices running the Android Open Source Project (AOSP) version. Google's report does not say how many certified devices were affected. When Google sued over the BadBox 2.0 botnet in July 2025, the more than 10 million devices involved were uncertified.

11bvteq.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a cyber espionage campaign targeting Israel and the Kurdistan Region of Iraq by an Iran state-aligned threat actor between August and October 2026. According to a report published by Dream Research Labs, the campaign has led to the compromise of a high-profile individual in Israel, along with additional compromises affecting a government cloud environment in the Kurdistan Region. The activity has been attributed to a threat actor known as DarkBlinders, an Iran-nexus group assessed to be active since at least September 2024 and linked to attacks aimed at aviation infrastructure and telecommunications in the U.A.E. and Iraq. It exhibits no technical overlap with other known hacking groups. Attacks mounted by the group are known to rely on spear-phishing as an initial access pathway to lure recipients into opening trojanized utilities or clicking on attacker-controlled websites that host similar tools as direct downloads. Previous attack chains documented by Elastic Security Labs and Group-IB have led to the deployment of SHELBYLOADER (aka HOTAIR), which is launched via DLL sideloading to ultimately execute a backdoor called SHELBYC2 (aka AEROSTAT) that uses GitHub for command-and-control (C2), data exfiltration, and remote control. Elastic is tracking the threat cluster under the moniker REF8685. Then early last month, Palo Alto Networks shed light on a campaign dubbed Blinder Tunnel in which the threat actor, which it calls CL-STA-1178, was observed masquerading as the Dubai Airports IT department to distribute malware-laced coding challenges to high-value targets. The bogus recruitment scheme was first detected in late March 2026, although evidence indicates that the attackers were staging and testing attack infrastructure as far back as November 2025. The social engineering campaign is assessed to have approached specific targets with lucrative job offers to trick them into executing a self-contained application that mimicked a career portal and instructed them to complete a questionnaire. Submitting the questionnaire does not cause any data to be exfiltrated or initiate any response from an external domain. Instead, it's meant to serve as a harmless decoy and build credibility before delivering the next stage payload containing the malware in the form of a Microsoft Visual Studio project archive that's dressed up as a coding assessment. The attack chain makes use of three techniques to establish persistent access: A malicious C# project ".csproj" file is used to trigger AppDomainManager injection, followed by DLL sideloading to deliver an updated version of SHELBYLOADER (aka ShelbyLoader V2), which then launches SHELBYC2. Also deployed via SHELBYC2 is a tunneling utility called Blackwood. "The attackers behind the activity used tailored social engineering techniques to masquerade as Dubai Airports recruiters, using a trojanized Visual Studio coding challenge to target a high-value job seeker based in Iraq," Unit 42 said. "The campaign is characterized by misuse of built-in developer tools and DLL sideloading. Attackers also used AppDomainManager hijacking to bypass security monitors like ETW [Event Tracing for Windows]." The latest findings from Dream show that the threat actor continues to rely on social engineering, while combining both credential phishing and malware delivery. This involves the use of government, webmail, and cloud-service lookalike domains to collect credentials or present attacker-controlled file downloads. Some of the highlighted domains include - gcc-sg[.]cloud/owa/auth/logon.aspx mfakuwait[.]online/owa/auth/logon.aspx moelcloud[.]online/drive/file/d/1JpH3ySmJpvX6TyGnF7C-S8qYiaoxyC5O The threat actor has also been observed setting decoy brand domains for a fake videoconferencing application called StarkMeet (stark-meet[.]com, stark-meet[.]online, and stark-meet[.]website). Installing and launching the app leads to the execution of ShelbyLoader V2 and SHELBYC2. The development is also a sign that the threat actor is trying out different methods for malware delivery, ranging from coding assessments to counterfeit software. Dream said the DarkBlinders activity belongs to the same operational cluster as UNC5795 and Dust Specter, citing infrastructure and malware overlaps. Dust Specter, documented by Zscaler in March 2026, refers to a suspected Iran-nexus operation targeting government officials in Iraq by impersonating the country's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. "Historical server fingerprints, overlapping victimology, and supporting attribution research lead us to assess with medium confidence that UNC5795 and UNC5187 may represent related sub-clusters within the broader APT34 group," it added. "Their overlapping focus on Iraqi government entities adds context to this technical connection and suggests a shared intelligence collection interest. Combined with their respective APT34 associations, these findings support a medium-confidence assessment that the two clusters are operationally related and may belong to the same broader group." Prince of Persia Hosts C2 in the U.S. for the First Time in a Decade The disclosure comes as Prince of Persia (aka Infy), a lesser-known threat group sponsored by the Iranian government, has been observed running one of its C2 servers ("68.65.122[.]203") from the U.S. this year. The server was likely built in July 2026. The infrastructure is a second-stage C2 server associated with Tornado, a Tonnerre variant that's dropped via one-day software vulnerabilities and uses both HTTPS and the Telegram API for C2. The emergence of new C2 servers in late May 2026 follows three months of inactivity, which has been described as the "longest downtime in nearly two decades of activity by the threat actor." "We have been monitoring Prince of Persia's exfiltration activity for the past six months," Tomer Bar, associate vice president of security research at Semperis, said. "The number of victims remains low, which could indicate either targeted attacks or difficulties infecting new victims." "The Iranian threat actor decided to host its new C2 server on U.S. soil — at the same time as the beginning of the recent hostilities between Iran and the United States. This is the last place we expected to find the threat actor hiding."

1jr16tz.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 02, 2026Vulnerability / Artificial Intelligence Two critical flaws in Langflow could let a remote attacker with no account bypass authentication or run arbitrary code, IBM said last week. Langflow is an open-source tool for building AI agents and workflows, and its vulnerability reports go to IBM. Every release from 1.0.0 through 1.12.8 has the flaws, and the only fix is version 1.13.0. Neither flaw is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, as of the catalog's October 30 update. Six other Langflow flaws are listed there, most recently CVE-2026-9198, which was added in August. The four Langflow flaws in IBM's bulletin, first published on October 28 and updated the next day, are: CVE CVSS score (IBM) Account needed What IBM says it could allow CVE-2026-93680 9.8 (Critical) No Bypassing security restrictions, because of improper authentication CVE-2026-110186 9.8 (Critical) No Running arbitrary code, because of improper control of code generation CVE-2026-110193 8.8 (High) Yes, a low-privileged account Making the Agentic Assistant generate or submit component code that runs operating system commands on the server CVE-2026-110192 6.5 (Medium) Yes Getting sensitive information from insufficiently protected credentials One of the flaws is "unauthenticated remote code execution exploitable through model context protocol tool enumeration," according to IBM. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Langflow can offer its flows as tools to AI apps that support MCP. A module in the public Metasploit Framework already cites CVE-2026-93680, the authentication bypass. It connects to a Langflow server's MCP endpoint without credentials, starts a session, and lists the tools the server offers. It does not run code or commands on the server. Its author lists Langflow 1.5.0 through 1.11.4 as affected, a narrower range than IBM's. When automatic login is enabled, Langflow logs users in as superusers without prompting them to sign in. The setting LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN is enabled by default in Langflow 1.12.8. Its code description warns that it "bypasses authentication and should only be used in development environments." The module was tested on Langflow 1.8.4 with automatic login turned on. Another of the four flaws is "an incomplete remediation of an auto-login security control," according to IBM. The bulletin does not say whether servers with automatic login turned off are vulnerable. Upgrading to 1.13.0 Langflow 1.13.0 came out on October 22. Version 1.12.8, released the same day, still has the flaws, and PyPI lists no later 1.12 release as of November 2. IBM offers no workaround for servers that cannot upgrade yet. Langflow 1.13 turns automatic login off by default. To upgrade: Back up the database, the secret key and uploaded files. If the server uses automatic login, prepare the existing account for password sign-in, as Langflow's upgrade guidance describes. Upgrade the Python package with pip install --upgrade "langflow==1.13.0". For Docker, move to the langflowai/langflow:1.13.0 image and keep the deployment's persistent data. If you cannot sign in after upgrading, follow the recovery steps that the same guidance links to. Do not delete or reinstall Langflow to get access back, because Langflow's documentation warns this can permanently remove your flows. On October 29, IBM also published CVE records for 29 other Langflow flaws and named versions 1.12.4 and 1.12.5 as their fixes. One of them, CVE-2026-104339, could also let an attacker with no account run arbitrary code, and IBM rates it 9.8. None of the 33 records, these four included, lists 1.13.0 as affected.

mgox6z.text: Forty percent of security teams now use AI every day, and another 56% are testing it. Only 4% have no plans to adopt it, according to Prophet Security's State of AI in Security Operations 2026 survey of more than 250 CISOs, SOC leaders and practitioners. For the teams still testing, the next decision is whether their own SOC is ready. AI SOC readiness has two parts: whether a SOC has the problems AI SOC agents are built for, and whether it has the data access, context, written standards and oversight rules that AI agents need to investigate alerts accurately in its environment. A SOC does not need to be far along a maturity model to be ready. AI agents do their first work on the bottom layer, alert handling, and the analyst hours they return give a team room to work on the layers above it. The next section describes those problems. Technical readiness covers four areas: access and context, an investigation standard with baseline metrics, rules for what the agent may do, and a plan for the time it gives back. Which SOCs benefit the most from AI SOC agents The SOCs that gain the most from AI SOC agents usually recognize several of the problems below, whether an outside provider works their alerts or their own analysts do. If an MDR or MSSP works your alerts: Your MDR flags threats too slowly. The provider works your alerts in a queue it shares with its other customers, so the escalation for a real intrusion can arrive hours after the activity started. Your MDR hands alerts back for lack of context. An escalation arrives with a short summary and questions such as is this login expected, is this a production server, or is this user traveling? The provider often does not know your users, assets and business well enough to finish the investigation, so your analysts do the rest. Your MDR closes alerts without showing its work. When the provider marks an alert benign, the note may not say what it checked and how it came to that conclusion, so your team either trusts the call or runs the investigation again. Your MDR's coverage stops at the tools it supports. Many contracts cover the EDR and a set list of log sources, so alerts from everything else, such as a SaaS application or a second cloud platform, land on your team. If your own analysts work the queue, including whatever the provider sends back: "Are we impacted?" takes days to answer. When a critical vulnerability or a new campaign makes the news, leadership wants an answer the same day. Getting one means hunting across the environment by hand, usually by an analyst who is also working the queue. Lower-severity alerts wait or get closed in bulk. A thorough investigation means pivoting across the SIEM, EDR, identity provider, cloud console and email tools, so the team keeps up with critical and high alerts and gets to the rest when it can. In the survey, 60% of respondents said an alert they had ignored or missed later turned into a serious issue, such as a breach or downtime. Noisy detections get switched off. Tuning a rule that fires too often takes time the team does not have, so the rule gets disabled and the technique it watched goes uncovered. Hunting and detection engineering wait for spare time. Proactive work happens when someone has a free afternoon, because the alert queue comes first. A few senior analysts carry the hard cases. Only one or two people know how to work the most difficult investigations, so a single resignation can set the team back. Nights and weekends are thinly covered. Staffing the queue around the clock takes more analysts than the budget covers, so alerts that fire after hours wait until morning or go to whoever is on call. AI SOC agents are built for this work. They are designed to start on each alert as it arrives, whichever tool raised it and at whatever hour. They can pull the context an outside provider lacks from your own systems and record the evidence behind each conclusion, so your team can check it. Some can also run a hunt the day a new threat is disclosed, which turns "are we impacted?" into a set of queries with answers. The analyst hours they return can go to the detection and hunting work that waits today. If several of these problems sound familiar, the need is there. The next question is whether your SOC can support a deployment. Where AI agents fit on a SOC maturity model Prophet Security's SOC maturity model, the SOC Hierarchy of Needs, has five levels: alert management, detection coverage, threat awareness, proactive hunting and posture improvements. Each level depends on the one below it. A team buried in alerts rarely gets to hunting, and a team that hunts without threat awareness has no clear idea what to look for. Many SOCs have not yet stabilized the first level. In the State of AI in Security Operations 2026 survey, respondents said 28% of their alerts are never investigated. AI SOC agents usually start at that first level, investigating alerts as they arrive. Newer platforms also run hunts and propose detections, work that reaches into levels two and four. Either way, the analyst hours they return go to work above the first level, so readiness depends on what the first level needs. An AI agent can only investigate what it can query An AI agent investigates by running queries against your tools, so it cannot see anything it has no access to. If it can query the EDR but not the identity provider, it can describe what happened on the endpoint but not which account was behind it. Readiness here has three parts: API access to the sources an investigation needs. That usually means the SIEM, EDR, identity provider, cloud platforms, email and key SaaS applications. Context the agent can read. An agent needs asset criticality, user roles, VIP lists, business units and known-benign activity, such as scheduled scans and admin scripts, to tell an attacker from a legitimate administrator. Healthy data pipelines. A silent or delayed log source can make an investigation look complete when key evidence is missing, so the health of the pipelines that feed investigations needs monitoring. A quick test: take five recent incidents and list every query a senior analyst ran to close them. Any query the agent could not run marks a gap to close before a pilot. Data access also raises the most common objection. In our survey, 44% of teams cited data privacy and how AI models are trained, the most frequent roadblock respondents named. Ask each vendor whether your data trains their models and where your data is processed. Define a finished investigation and record your baseline A pilot needs a written standard to grade the agent against. In many SOCs, only senior analysts know that standard, and it is rarely written down. The standard covers which evidence closes a phishing case, when an impossible-travel alert needs a call to the user's manager, and what counts as enough to call an alert benign. Writing it down for your highest-volume alert types also gives new analysts an onboarding document. Also keep a list of the detections that were switched off. In our survey, up to 40% of organizations had turned off some detections because they lacked the people to check them. When an agent investigates every alert, some of those rules can come back, and the list tells you where to start. Then record the numbers you will compare against: the share of alerts investigated, mean time to investigate, time from alert to first look, and how often closed alerts are reopened. The survey gives a reference point. A thorough investigation takes an average of 75 minutes, and alerts often wait close to an hour before anyone opens them. You can download our guide on detection engineering to learn more about how an agentic SOC benefits detection engineering. Decide what the agent may do, and who approves more Investigation and action carry different risks, and most teams treat them differently. In the survey, 57% of teams require a human to review every AI decision before an alert is closed. On response, 44% have AI recommend actions that people carry out, 30% let it handle low-risk remediation on its own, and no respondent gives it full, unsupervised autonomy. A ready SOC has these rules written down before a pilot starts: Default approvals. A list of the actions that stay human-approved, such as isolating a host, disabling an account or blocking a domain. How permissions widen. Who can grant the agent more autonomy for a category of action, and what track record they need to see first. Where findings land. Agent findings should appear in the case management or ticketing tools analysts already use, so nobody has to watch another console. Who owns feedback. A named person reviews the agent's mistakes and turns corrections into guidance it will use next time. Starting with read-only access for investigations, then widening permissions as confidence grows, applies the same rules a SOC uses for a new human analyst. Prophet Security's framework for building trust in an AI SOC follows the same stepwise approach. A readiness checklist mapped to the maturity model Answer each question yes or no. Part 1 checks the need, and Part 2 checks technical readiness. The level in parentheses shows which layer of the SOC Hierarchy of Needs each item belongs to. Part 1: Does your SOC need AI SOC agents? Do escalations from your MDR or MSSP arrive hours after the activity started? (Level 1: alert management) Does your provider hand alerts back because it lacked the context to finish them? (Level 3: threat awareness) Does your provider close alerts without showing what it checked? (Level 1: alert management) Do alerts from tools outside your provider's coverage land on your team? (Level 1: alert management) Does it take more than a day to tell leadership whether you are impacted by a new vulnerability or campaign? (Level 4: proactive hunting) Do low- and medium-severity alerts wait, or get closed in bulk without an investigation? (Level 1: alert management) Have noisy detections been switched off because no one had time to tune them? (Level 2: detection coverage) Do hunting and detection engineering wait until someone has spare time? (Level 4: proactive hunting) Do only one or two senior analysts know how to work your hardest cases? (Level 1: alert management) Do alerts that fire at night or on weekends wait until morning? (Level 1: alert management) Each yes is a problem an AI SOC agent can take on, and the more yes answers, the stronger the case for a deployment. Part 2: Is your SOC ready to deploy them? Can a new tool query your SIEM, EDR, identity, cloud and email sources through an API? (Level 1: alert management) Are asset criticality, user roles and known-benign activity recorded somewhere a system can read? (Level 3: threat awareness) Is there a written standard for what a complete investigation includes, for the alert types that make up most of your volume? (Level 1: alert management) Have you decided which actions stay human-approved, and who can widen the agent's permissions? (Level 1: alert management) Do you monitor whether the log sources your investigations depend on are arriving? (Level 2: detection coverage) Do you know your current share of alerts investigated and your mean time to investigate? (Level 1: alert management) Do you keep a list of detections that were switched off for capacity reasons? (Level 2: detection coverage) Is there a plan, with named owners, for the analyst hours an agent will return, such as scheduled hunts or detection work? (Level 4: proactive hunting) A "no" on any of the first four is worth fixing before a production pilot. The other four can be worked on during it. What to do if the answer is not yet Most items on the Part 2 list are configuration and documentation work: issuing API credentials, exporting asset and user context, and writing down the investigation standard. A workable order: Close the access gaps from the five-incident test first, since every later step depends on the agent seeing the data. Write the investigation standards for your highest-volume alert types. Run the agent in parallel with your analysts for a few weeks. Record the baseline before it starts, and treat every analyst override as data about where the agent needs more context. Widen the agent's permissions one category of action at a time, as its record supports it. Some teams that are not ready consider building their own agents instead. The survey suggests caution: 72% of AI users had tried building internal AI tools, and 46% of those projects were abandoned, never reached production, or were replaced by a commercial product. Building a functioning prototype is only a small chunk of the work. Most of the work is engineering and maintenance of integrations that take weeks to build but break when a vendor changes an API; rate limits to work around; model deprecations every six to nine months that force a full round of evals, guardrails, and prompt injection testing; and audit trails explaining why each alert was closed. How Prophet Security Works Prophet Security is the leading AI SOC platforms for enterprise SOCs, recognized in Rising in Cyber 2026, an honor voted on by more than 150 CISOs and security leaders. Its platform, Prophet AI, works from the stack a team already runs. First-generation AI SOC tools stopped at alert triage. Prophet AI enables an agentic SOC, with specialist agents for investigation, threat hunting and detection engineering. Prophet AI SOC Analyst investigates every alert at every severity, around the clock, with the depth of a senior analyst. It queries SIEM, EDR, identity, cloud and email tools directly and records every question, query and piece of evidence behind a determination, so an analyst can rerun any query and check the work. It takes response actions only within permissions the customer sets, with human approval as the default. Prophet AI Threat Hunter is built to answer "are we impacted?" It keeps a profile of each organization's industry, technology stack and the threat actors that target it. When a severe new threat emerges, hunts for it run automatically in the background. Scheduled hunts, including hunts against coverage gaps and questions the team writes in plain language, run on the cadence the team sets. Suspicious leads go to the SOC Analyst for a full investigation. Prophet AI Detection Engineer takes on the detection engineering work that waits for spare time. It keeps a live MITRE ATT&CK coverage map built from the organization's own investigations, showing which techniques are covered, which have gone quiet and which are dark. It builds and tunes detections from what investigations, hunts and coverage gaps reveal, writes them in the rule language of the SIEM or tool they run in, and backtests each one against the organization's own history. Each change arrives as a reviewable proposal with its rationale and backtest results, and by default nothing reaches production until the team approves it. Each product's findings feed the others. Investigations show which detections are noisy and where coverage is thin, hunts look in those gaps, and what the hunts find becomes new detections. The team teaches Prophet AI in plain language, and that guidance shapes how investigations run, how hunts are scoped and how detections are written. Customer data never trains its models, and the data plane can run inside the customer's own VPC.
