u52t7u.text: Attackers posing as IT support on Microsoft Teams talked employees into giving them remote control of their PCs. They then used insecure Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) settings to obtain login certificates for privileged accounts, including one for a domain controller. Microsoft said in a report that it investigated two such intrusions, one of which resulted in company data being copied to an external server. The attackers exploited no flaw in Teams itself. They relied on social engineering and on AD CS that had been set up insecurely, and Microsoft did not tie the activity to any known group. How the Attacks Began Both intrusions started the same way, Microsoft said. The attackers messaged and called employees on Teams while posing as the company's own IT or help desk, working from outside tenants with support-themed names so the contact looked familiar. They talked each user into opening Quick Assist, a remote-help tool built into Windows, and reading the connection code back to them. That gave the attacker direct, hands-on control of the workstation. From there, the attacker dropped an archive into the Downloads folder, unpacked it into a new folder named to resemble a Windows update, and ran its contents with a portable Python, Bun, or Java runtime. File names alone were a weak signal, because one copy was renamed while still carrying the real runtime's version details. What a Certificate Buys an Attacker AD CS is the Windows role that issues the certificates users and computers present when they log in. A certificate from a poorly configured template lets whoever holds it sign in as the account it names. Microsoft said such a certificate continues to work even after the account's password is reset or the first machine is wiped, so neither step ends the attacker's access. Case 1: Privileged Certificates, and a Gap in Containment In the first intrusion, the attackers found a certificate template with a weakness known as ESC1. With that kind of template, the requester can name the account the certificate will represent, so a low-privileged user can request one that stands in for a privileged account. The first wave of calls targeted three users and one workstation, producing certificates for three highly privileged accounts. Microsoft Defender's automatic attack disruption cut those identities off and dropped their active sessions. One privileged account, though, had been left out of the automatic response, so it stayed usable. About 90 minutes later, a larger wave hit 16 users and a second workstation, producing certificates for 8 more privileged accounts. Microsoft said more than 1,000 later attempts to reach files over SMB or to log in were blocked. Within seconds of obtaining a certificate, the attacker signed in to a domain controller and ran DCSync, a tool for copying password data from Active Directory. The operation had already begun when containment took hold, limiting how much could be replicated. Microsoft did not say how much credential data the attacker obtained. The excluded account was the opening. The attacker kept using it, reached a file server, and ran a renamed copy of the file-copying tool Rclone to move data from a share to an outside SFTP server. Microsoft did not say how much data was taken. The case shows, in Microsoft's words, that "partial identity containment can reduce attack activity while still leaving a viable privileged route." Case 2: A Certificate for the Domain Controller The second intrusion began the same way but took a different direction because that template weakness was not present. The attacker instead used a technique called PetitPotam to force a domain controller to authenticate to a machine the attacker controlled. That NTLM login was relayed to the AD CS web enrollment page, an abuse known as ESC8, with no password needed. The attacker used the relayed login to request a certificate for the domain controller itself. With that certificate and Kerberos (PKINIT), the attacker obtained a ticket-granting ticket for the domain controller, turning a one-off relayed login into a lasting identity. Here the response held. Defender raised ESC8 alerts, the customer isolated the workstation, and Microsoft said no further activity followed. The difference between the two came down to containment. In the first, automatic disruption blocked most of the attack, but the one excluded account stayed open. In the second, isolating a single workstation stopped it. What Defenders Can Do There is no patch, because nothing here was a software flaw. Microsoft's advice is about configuration and response. Have staff confirm any unexpected support request through a known internal channel before sharing a screen or handing over remote control. Limit which outside Teams tenants can reach employees, and allow only approved remote-support tools. Review sign-in certificate templates for ones that let the requester name the account, or that too many users can enroll in, and remove enrollment rights that are not needed. Require HTTPS and turn on Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on web enrollment endpoints, and turn off NTLM there where you can. Microsoft's KB5005413 covers this, and its Defender for Identity posture checks flag templates and endpoints exposed to ESC1 and ESC8. Turn on certificate auditing. If a bad certificate was issued, revoke it, but remember that revocation does not cancel Kerberos tickets already issued; review active tickets separately. Treat any account left out of automatic containment as a deliberate decision and assign a manual action in its place. What Is and Isn't Known Microsoft did not attribute the intrusions to any named group and did not give the dates on which they happened. The methods are not new. Researchers named the ESC1 and ESC8 certificate weaknesses in 2021, and the PetitPotam coercion trick was disclosed the same year. Microsoft itself had documented the Teams help-desk-to-remote-access entry method earlier in 2026. What this report adds is that the two techniques meet in real intrusions, along with the lesson about the excluded account. Newer Windows is less exposed to the ESC8 step. Microsoft turned EPA on by default for AD CS in Windows Server 2025, whereas Server 2022 and 2019 require it to be enabled manually. Indicators and Detections Microsoft's report lists Defender alerts across Teams, endpoints, and identity signals, and four advanced hunting queries that it calls "starting points for investigation" rather than proof on their own. It also published three file hashes tied to the initial-access scripts: SHA-256 85b6c424117494d3056e88689dbc94c75e9afdb187a339714043aec0da109f17 (JavaScript initial-access script) SHA-256 f326201269f1ee2f803ae435317507263bb6e0dbfdeb70bd1bb5446e2e46f001 (Python initial-access script) SHA-256 06c5c14f043aee3bcc5843b5f50909623d5c9a6239a7c1fba9cddad4111469e7 (Python initial-access script)

1pwvgn8.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a cyber espionage campaign specifically targeting Linux infrastructure associated with government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure. The activity, observed by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 between October 2025 and April 2026, has been tracked under the moniker CL-UNK-1211, where "CL" refers to cluster and "UNK" stands for unknown motivation. A notable aspect of the campaign concerns the use of large language models (LLMs) and/or automated artificial intelligence (AI) agents to generate payloads and execute malicious code. "The attackers behind this cluster of activity focused on Linux environments to conduct extensive reconnaissance and maintain persistent network access to support intelligence-gathering," researchers Roey Porat and Tom Fakterman said. "The attackers attempted to dump sensitive databases and exfiltrate government mailboxes to access social media accounts." The campaign employs a "versatile operational playbook," leveraging a combination of open-source tools, custom cross-platform backdoors, and web shells to maintain access. Another hallmark involves attempts to disable endpoint protections, wipe system logs, and plant deceptive red-team markers so as to disguise the activity as a legitimate security assessment. The threat actor has also been observed using malicious PHP and shell scripts, likely generated using AI, to maintain persistence, perform reconnaissance, and exfiltrate data. "Rather than standard developer documentation, multiple scripts contained conversational, step-by-step reasoning notes. These notes explained the code's logic to the operator who provided the initial instructions," the cybersecurity company said. "Their presence suggests that the code was either copied directly from an AI prompt output or deployed by an automated AI agent." A mix of open-source and bespoke PHP web shells is used as a way to maintain a persistent backdoor into the host networks. The access is then abused to gather credentials from the targeted environment using three different methods - Replacing the .bashrc file with a malicious version containing a command to steal passwords. Injecting code into PHP login pages to harvest admin credentials. Scanning for cleartext email, SMTP, and database passwords within configuration files and command history files. Also deployed as part of the attacks is a custom, multi-platform remote access trojan written in Go that supports various persistence methods to maintain long-term access on Windows and Linux systems. Called SysGoRAT, it establishes a command-and-control (C2) connection over WebSocket to a hard-coded IP address ("104.194.158[.]65:443") and fetches seven types of commands - command, to execute arbitrary commands via /bin/sh -c (Linux) or cmd /C (Windows) control, to spawn via sub-commands an interactive shell (shell_start), screenshots (screenshot), exfiltrate files to the C2 server (download), and install persistence (persist) list_dir, to list directory content shell_input, to create an interactive shell session proxy_connect, to establish a TCP connection to an arbitrary target proxy_data, to relay data bidirectionally to an established proxy connection proxy_close, to terminate and remove a proxy session Furthermore, the attacks make use of in-memory reverse shells to avoid leaving forensic artifacts on disk, as well as enumerate "/var/qmail/mailnames/" directories to count the number of emails stored in specific folders. "Next, the attackers searched for social media-related emails," Unit 42 explained. "They deployed a PHP script, named search_social.php, that searched for specific keywords in email headers and displayed the results in a user-friendly format." "The script then parsed the response and displayed the exact file path, social media account email sender, recipient and subject." The attackers have also been found attempting to generate a bash script named "zip_mails.sh" in a bid to compress emails of interest into ZIP archives and exfiltrate the information. However, syntax errors present in the script meant that the program failed upon execution. "This campaign demonstrates how attackers are combining traditional post-exploitation techniques with AI-accelerated workflows to target governmental Linux server infrastructure," Unit 42 said. "By leveraging AI to rapidly generate, adapt and deploy operational scripts, the attackers behind CL-UNK-1211 maintained a fast pace of operation while minimizing manual developer overhead." The development comes as Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, along with Microsoft, documented threat actors' abuse of open-source agentic penetration testing frameworks like ARTEX, PentAGI, Hexstrike, and CAIRN to carry out a "broad range of actions" across various stages of the attack life cycle at an unprecedented speed and scale. Although ARTEX was taken down by its author after reports of widespread misuse emerged, it has spawned multiple versions, including a commercial offering dubbed ARTEX PRO and a localized variation called ScopeWeaver. Some of the cases are listed below - Use of ARTEX by Storm-0940 (aka UNC7228) to orchestrate data theft campaigns targeting entities in the U.S. and Europe across the enterprise software, industrial automation, semiconductor manufacturing and design, and telecommunications industry verticals. Use of ARTEX by financially motivated threat actors to facilitate data theft extortion, including the targeting of the financial sector in Asia. Use of ARTEX by North Korean state-sponsored hacking groups like Onyx Sleet (aka Andariel) and Pearl Sleet (aka Lawrencium) in operations. Use of PentAGI for WHOIS asset mapping and systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against organizations in Asia. "The emergence of ARTEX and similar agentic offensive intrusion frameworks underscores a broader shift toward threat actor adoption of open source multi-agent offensive frameworks, as well as potentially custom agentic harnesses," GTIG and Mandiant said. "Frameworks such as ARTEX compress attack timelines to machine speed; however, they currently trade stealth for velocity. Unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic, relies on recognizable identifiers, and leaves behind distinct code-level traces, increasing the likelihood of detection and mitigation."

1809b1v.text: Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a new Windows infostealer malware called VOLTA-AUTODOXER (aka VOLTA) that makes use of a large language model (LLM) to rank a victim's stolen data by their monetization value. Like other typical stealer families, VOLTA is equipped to harvest passwords and cookies from Chromium-based web browsers; data from Outlook profiles and Slack workspaces; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots. "VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine," Cisco Talos researcher Ryan Fetterman said. "This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation." To make this information more valuable, the malware uses stolen session access to search the victim's Gmail account for receipts to corroborate the home address by extracting emails related to Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal. Once the necessary information is collected, the bundle is serialized and fed into an artificial intelligence (AI) system for analysis using OpenRouter, a unified LLM API gateway and routing service, along with a system prompt. The requests are defaulted to Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6, failing which it falls back to Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 and Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash. "VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model's refusal, checking each response for phrases like 'I can't' or 'I'm not able,' before passing on to a chain of up to three models," Talos said. VOLTA features a 240-word system prompt that instructs the model to assume the role of a "forensic intelligence analyst" responsible for drafting a target assessment based on data from a structured evidence bundle. "The bundle is the ONLY permissible source of facts; your training knowledge must never supply a fact about the subject," reads a line from the prompt. "The required output includes a section titled 'WHAT THEY'RE WORTH' with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on 'THEIR OPSEC' containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene," Talos explained. "The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets." Data exfiltration happens over Telegram at three different stages - Right after the stealer runs, containing details about browser passwords, cookies, payment cards, cryptocurrency wallets; Discord, Steam, and Roblox tokens; Wi-Fi passwords, and screenshots After the AI call, which includes the captured data and the results of the LLM analysis After the live enrichment step, which includes Gmail receipts and order histories What's more, VOLTA makes use of a template containing six slots that are filled in at build time. This includes the Telegram channel used for data exfiltration, API keys, and other settings. This approach suggests that the malware author is likely either advertising a builder kit to prospective customers or operating it as a bespoke tool under their control to compile a custom binary for each order. "If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations," Talos said. "It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox." "VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement." The disclosure comes as adversarial adoption of generative AI (aka GenAI) is quickly becoming the new normal, as threat actors incorporate the technology into their workflows to develop custom tools or find valuable data, thereby increasing the likelihood of success of their attacks. "GenAI technologies are also well suited to examine massive amounts of data for the purposes of classification or content searching," Zscaler ThreatLabz said. "Once an attacker has access to the victim’s system, GenAI can therefore be used to search all materials to which a victim's system has access, seeking the most valuable or sensitive data for theft or encryption during the next phase of the attack." A ransomware actor can leverage this method to identify and acquire the most sensitive data from a compromised network, maximizing the chances that the victim will pay up. Last week, Talos also detailed an AI-enabled framework called NIK C2 that gives attackers remote access, credential theft, keylogging, defense evasion, surveillance, and ransomware capabilities, while integrating an OpenAI client to send stolen data for AI analysis within the compromised session. A Go-based, Windows remote access tool, NIK C2 grants persistent control over compromised hosts and supports over 52 commands sent by a command-and-control (C2) server to collect a wide range of data. The OpenAI integration is notable for the fact that the threat actor can abuse a victim's own OpenAI API key to execute the AI-driven analysis. Specifically, the plant checks if the actor has supplied an API key. In the absence of one, it scans the victim's environment variables for the string "OPENAI_API_KEY" and uses it. This is a form of LLMjacking, where bad actors steal access to another party's AI model to run their own operations – in this case, against the victim itself – while the legitimate owner pays for the computing power. In addition, it allows the attacker to evade detection by obscuring who made the requests. "This fallback is not a backup mechanism for API key resolution. It is a deliberate design with significant operational implications," Talos said. "If the victim has configured an OpenAI account on their machine, that account's API key will be used to fund the actor's AI inference." "NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that historically granted defenders critical detection windows," Talos said.

azxhye.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 01, 2026Vulnerability / Cloud Security A critical flaw in Canonical's LXD and MicroCloud let an attacker log in as a trusted client without holding that client's private key. To do it, the attacker had to reach their HTTPS API over the network and have the trusted client's public certificate. Once in, the attacker would act as that client, with access to the cluster and its virtual machines. If the impersonated account is privileged, the attacker could gain "root access to the host machine," Canonical said. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-112816, carries a maximum CVSS score of 10.0, and Canonical has released fixed versions of both products. How the Flaw Works LXD and MicroCloud let remote clients access their APIs over mutual TLS, a setup in which the client presents a certificate to prove who it is. A client is trusted when its certificate is in the server's trust store, the list of identities the server will accept. The flaw was in how the server checked that certificate. It compared every certificate the client sent against the trust store, but a TLS connection only proves the client owns the private key for the first certificate in the chain, the leaf. The rest of the chain is whatever the client chose to attach. So an attacker could take a trusted client's public certificate, which is not secret, attach it to the chain behind their own, and the server would accept them as that client. Who Is Affected Using the flaw takes two things: network access to the HTTPS API, and the public certificate of a client the server already trusts. A standalone LXD server does not expose that API by default. It listens only on a local socket unless an administrator turns on the network API with the core.https_address setting. MicroCloud, which ties several machines running LXD into one cluster, has a specific weak point. Canonical said an attacker who can capture a member's public certificate as it joins the cluster can then log in as that member. The CVE record lists LXD 4.0.14, 5.0.10, 5.21.8 and 6.9 as affected, each before the fixed release that follows. Canonical lists these fixed snap versions: Product Snap channel Fixed version LXD 6/stable 6.10.1 LXD 5.21/stable 5.21.9 LXD 5.0/stable 5.0.11 LXD 4.0/stable 4.0.15 MicroCloud 3/stable 3.4.1 MicroCloud 2/stable 2.1.5 The bug did not start at Canonical. The Incus project, which began as a community fork of LXD, reported it, and Canonical confirmed it affected LXD as well. Incus fixed the same flaw in version 7.6.0. Ubuntu's own archive packages of LXD are listed as not affected or not shipped, so the fixed releases are the snaps. There is no public sign the flaw has been used in an attack. The CVE record carries a U.S. CISA assessment, dated October 30, that the flaw is not known to have been exploited; it is not on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, and no working exploit has been published. What to Do Update LXD and MicroCloud to the fixed versions. On a snap install, run sudo snap refresh lxd and sudo snap refresh microcloud. Canonical said the fixed LXD point releases were still rolling out from the candidate channel to stable at the time of its advisory, so check the version you actually have after the refresh rather than assume the fix arrived. Canonical's advisory gives no temporary workaround for LXD. Because the attack requires network access to the API, limiting who can reach it reduces risk until you update. The Incus project, reporting the same flaw, said there is no configuration fix and that the only step is to restrict network access to the listener. Incus users should move to 7.6.0, which fixed this flaw along with 17 other security issues.

1r5yhjg.text: Malicious code on the website of prediction market Polymarket sold some signed-in traders' positions and moved their funds to the hackers on October 29. The code had replaced a page-speed script that the site loaded from an outside company. Polymarket says it is refunding about $2.7 million to 726 affected wallets. Blockchain records show crypto worth about $2.64 million reached the hackers' wallet in under an hour. The replaced script came from DebugBear, whose real user monitoring (RUM) tool measures how fast web pages load for real visitors. Researchers at Hudson Rock downloaded the malicious file on October 29 from the address Polymarket's site used to load the DebugBear script. They also found a change in Polymarket's site code that removed the DebugBear script. DebugBear's DNS records were compromised through its domain registrar, the company said on X. Its early findings indicate the attack targeted one customer's website. It has seen no sign of a break-in to its own systems, though it is still looking. Researchers at Ohey found a different server answering for DebugBear's web addresses at 18:13 UTC, when the malicious file was still online. Earlier that day, the normal script had been served from Google Cloud Storage. Each DebugBear customer loads its own copy of the script, and the file that was swapped was Polymarket's. How the Script Took the Money The code reuses the access a signed-in trader already has in an open Polymarket page, Hudson Rock found after reviewing the file without running it. It reads account details that Polymarket keeps in the browser, including a set of trading API keys. Those API keys alone cannot place an order on Polymarket, because orders also need a wallet signature. Hudson Rock found no part of the code that sends the keys, a password, a seed phrase, or a private key to the server it reports to. Instead, the code searches the page for the part of Polymarket's site that places orders, and for the signer that approves the account's transactions. It then takes one of two paths. For accounts that sign in with their own crypto wallet, it moves the trader's positions straight to the hackers' wallet. For accounts that sign in via email, it sells positions at ever-worse prices and then moves the money out. In both paths, the code asks the account's own signer to sign its requests and hands them to Polymarket's relayer, which submits them. Hudson Rock said a signing request alone does not prove a trader signed without seeing a prompt. The wallet provider may still ask the trader, refuse, or apply its own rules for the session. The wallet written into the code received its first funds at 17:10 UTC and its last at 18:02 UTC, according to Ohey's blockchain trace. In that time, it collected 28.6 million POL tokens and positions from 33 wallets. At 18:19 UTC, those 28.6 million POL were worth about $2.64 million at DefiLlama's price of $0.0922, DefiPrime calculated. The figure covers only the POL, not the positions. The wallet sent all 28.6 million POL on to three other addresses between 18:28 and 18:38 UTC, its transaction history shows. Polymarket's Response and Refunds Polymarket posted its first status update about unauthorized activity in user wallets at 17:38 UTC. At 18:05 UTC, it said its exchange was in cancel-only mode, with relayer actions paused. The company said it removed the script "within the hour." It also cleared every cache, reset all active login sessions and paused trading until the site was clean. It has referred the case to law enforcement. By October 30, 689 of the 726 affected wallets had been refunded in full, and the remaining 37 were being paid as they were checked. Polymarket is also paying $1.19 million to about 5,500 wallets that lost money during the trading pause or had positions taken. In all, it is returning $3.9 million to traders. Traders do not need to file a claim. Polymarket's status page links a form for anyone who thinks their amount is wrong or that they should have received a payment. What Sites and Traders Can Do DebugBear has told customers of its RUM product to remove its embed code from their websites. The address that served the malicious file, cdn.debugbear[.]com, had no DNS record when The Hacker News checked on November 1. Polymarket said it is putting third-party scripts back in place with extra checks, such as a stronger Content Security Policy (CSP), pinned versions, and sandboxing. Hudson Rock's advice for sites that load outside scripts: Keep unneeded third-party code off pages where users trade or sign. Where a file can be pinned, use Subresource Integrity (SRI), which lets the browser reject the file if its contents change. A security policy that simply allows a trusted CDN does not check the files that CDN serves. Check what code on a signed-in page can ask the signer to do. Hudson Rock's advice for traders is to reject any signing request they did not expect.

91ovzm.text: The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has officially attributed the theft of more than $6 billion in virtual assets to TraderTraitor, a North Korea-aligned elite hacking group also tracked as Jade Sleet, Pressure Chollima, PUKCHONG, Slow Pisces, and UNC4899. The FBI, along with the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), said it observed the threat actor converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH). "It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using DeFi and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages," the FBI said in a statement. The agency has also provided a list of wallet addresses that the attackers are said to be using to launder the stolen assets. The development comes as Binance said it has resumed phase one of withdrawals starting today between 6 and 9 a.m. UTC after they were paused in the wake of the incident. "Since the incident, our teams have taken precautionary measures to safeguard the platform, conducted security assessments, and worked to verify the readiness of affected services," Binance said in a statement. "We aim to restore withdrawals progressively as we complete security and readiness checks. Deposit services remain open and are not affected by the incident." The haul eclipses the $1.46 billion plundered from Bybit in February 2025, making it the largest cryptocurrency theft in history. The funds were stolen across 11 blockchains, 82% of which were on Ethereum and Bitcoin. "This single incident almost doubles the total cryptoassets stolen by the regime," blockchain analysis firm Elliptic said. "Actors linked to North Korea, officially the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK), are believed to have stolen over $6.5 billion in cryptoassets in recent years." Of the $6.43 billion stolen by TraderTraitor, $2.85 billion of the assets have been frozen on-chain by Tether, Circle, Ripple, Arbitrum, and Optimism. TraderTraitor is the name assigned to a North Korean group that has a history of orchestrating cryptocurrency thefts against the Web3.0 industry by tricking victims into downloading malware-laced applications. The cluster is known to be active since at least 2020. In recent years, the adversary has been attributed to cryptocurrency heists targeting DMM Bitcoin, Bybit, KelpDAO, and Bitget. Reports from SentinelOne, Zscaler ThreatLabz, and Microsoft have revealed that TraderTraitor is continuing to hone its tradecraft, using trojanized Terraform providers as a malware distribution vector and leveraging front companies to conduct job-themed targeting against individuals involved in cybersecurity, AI, blockchain, and talent recruitment companies. The poisoned Terraform provider is used to deliver a Bash loader that selects and downloads malware tailored to the victim's operating system. This includes a cross-platform implant called FLATROOF, which siphons sensitive data from the victim using a Python-based information stealer before ultimately dropping the ROOFDECK backdoor to obtain complete remote control. The activity once again demonstrates how North Korean threat actors continue to abuse trusted developer workflows through trojanized Terraform providers to deliver cross-platform malware across macOS, Linux, and Windows systems, and gain persistent access. TraderTraitor's modus operandi, like other North Korea-linked campaigns such as Lazarus Group's Operation Dream Job and Famous Chollima's Contagious Interview, employs recruitment-themed lures as a pretext to convince victims to run malicious code. The social engineering phase is augmented by the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to craft convincing lures, create fake personas, and evade detection. "The actor leveraged tailored domains, social media profiles, and industry-specific knowledge to pose as recruiters for a spoofed AI-powered blockchain intelligence company, using software engineer-themed opportunities to initiate contact and schedule interviews with individuals who engaged with the outreach," Microsoft said. "Within this short time frame, Jade Sleet conducted similar job-themed targeting using two additional front companies, supported by comparable infrastructure and relevant domain knowledge."

1ugojcw.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 01, 2026Windows Security / Cyber Espionage Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of what has been described as a "highly sophisticated infection chain" targeting government organizations in Asia. The activity, detailed by Kaspersky this week, targeted a custom Windows 10 build used exclusively by government entities in Asia and involves the deployment of a previously undocumented .NET assembly-loading framework codenamed NetamLoader. The attack has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. Nor is it clear if the intrusion compromised more than one system and allowed the hackers to steal any sensitive information. The Russian cybersecurity company said the artifact was detected in the first half of 2026, packaged inside a Windows cabinet archive (CAB) file placed in a directory that stores Windows operating system update packages. It's suspected the operation involved a supply chain attack, in which bad actors compromised a trusted third-party vendor to gain access to downstream users who rely on its services or software. The sample in question features a ".config" file that employs AppDomainManager injection to load arbitrary .NET assemblies. AppDomainManager injection is an adversarial technique used to load arbitrary payloads by hijacking .NET Framework's AppDomainManager mechanism when a .NET application starts. Put differently, the approach targets .NET Framework's application-domain initialization to achieve code execution. The end result is the same as DLL sideloading: to run malicious code inside a legitimate application's process so as to fly under the radar. According to Kaspersky, the CAB archive containing the .config file was placed in the path: "C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\e4537a1762fcafd2fd96bfc825bad34f9db9a24," with its contents extracted and dropped into "C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\Install\." Infection chain: Stage 1 The exact delivery vehicle for the CAB archive remains unknown. Present in the archive are seven files, four of which are legitimate components of Patch My PC, an endpoint management software - fabric.config Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll PatchMyPC-Enum.dll PatchMyPC-Models.dll PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config Resources.resx None of the files with the exception of "Resources.resx" embed malicious code. The infection chain plays out as a two-stage process as follows - The execution of "PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe" serves as the launchpad for several payloads. It abuses AppDomainManager injection to parse "PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config," resulting in the execution of "Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll." Once loaded, "Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll" finds "fabric.config" located in the same directory and parses its contents to load "Resources.resx." "Resources.resx" contains "multiple layers" of encoded, compressed, or encrypted payloads, such as XAML files, .NET assemblies, and JSON data, which are decoded and loaded by the component before it. Infection chain: Stage 2 A brief description of these payloads is listed below - XAML-1, a loader for an embedded payload, XAML-2. XAML‑2 initializes the second stage of the attack chain by loading two compressed and Base64‑encoded XAML files: XAML-2-1 and XAML-2-2. XAML-2-1 is used to bypass Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI). XAML-2-2 contains two parts, a .NET module (aka .NET 1 Loader) and a JSON data payload (aka JSON-1). JSON-1, the JSON payload that contains two components: JSON-1-c, which stores command-and-control (C2) server configuration, and JSON-1-p, which contains a Base64‑encoded file (.NET 2 Plugin) and a collection of compressed, encrypted XAML templates used to build XAML-3. XAML-2-2 loads .NET 1 Loader, which then serves as a decrypting, assembling, and loading for XAML‑3, reports the status to the C2 server, and deletes malicious files extracted from the CAB archive, along with CLR usage logs and Windows system Prefetch cache files to cover up the tracks. XAML-3, the XAML payload that runs within "dllhost.exe" and is designed to decode, decompress, and load .NET 2 Plugin. .NET 2 Plugin, a .NET assembly that loads the C2 configuration, gathers system information from Windows Registry, checks if the current host process is "dllhost.exe," waits a random jitter delay of 20-40 minutes before issuing its first request to the C2 server ("openaigpt4v[.]com"), and enters into a periodic polling loop to fetch an XAML file and execute it in an isolated AppDomain. "If a valid response is received from C2, the loop pauses for 5-6 minutes before the next request; otherwise, it pauses for 22-28 hours, checking every 10 minutes to determine whether the allotted time has elapsed," Kaspersky explained. Telemetry data gathered by Kaspersky has identified a single victim in Asia, with NetamLoader designed to attack a Windows 10 build customized for government-only use. Although the targeted Asian country was not disclosed, signs are that it's likely China, as Microsoft offers a bespoke version called Windows 10 China Government Edition specifically for the Chinese government and state-owned entities. Earlier this August, Bloomberg reported that China's Ministry of State Security had ordered some government agencies to stop using the "Government Edition" in favor of Chinese-made Linux distributions as part of an effort to reduce its dependence on foreign technology. "Beijing's instruction stemmed from data security concerns," Bloomberg said, citing "people familiar with the matter." No additional details were disclosed at the time. "In today's geopolitical climate, a growing number of countries are building their own core software platforms, including operating systems, databases, middleware, and cloud services, with operating systems often the top priority," Kaspersky concluded. "The advantage is that each country controls the development, operation, and upgrading of its own operating systems, granting it full autonomy over the entire process. On the other hand, it also means that each country must protect this entire vast ecosystem on its own. Bringing the operation and maintenance of such a system to maturity is a lengthy process."

blz0sp.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 31, 2026Data Security / Cyber Attack American blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said it was the target of a cybersecurity incident in which an external actor accessed non-sensitive customer data. However, the company noted that the breach did not result in unauthorized access to its investigation content, authentication credentials, or session tokens. "This month, Chainalysis detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools," Chainalysis said Friday. "Some non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed, including such information relating to your organization and users." The company said it's patching vulnerabilities and hardening its systems in response to the incident. The mention of "offensive agentic techniques" indicates that an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered tool was used to execute the attack, although Chainalysis offered no details on the specific methods or tactics employed. "We are seeing an industry-wide rise in AI-driven cyber attacks, and we are taking a whole-of-company approach to make sure our security posture meets the evolving environment and our customers' expectations," it said. The development comes as adversarial use of AI has ramped up in recent months, with various threat actors using the technology to automate different stages of the attack lifecycle and target hundreds of organizations across multiple industries. This includes a China state-backed threat group known as Vapor Panda, which is using ARTEX, an agentic penetration testing framework, to conduct attacks at scale, compromising about 140 targets in a span of 11 days as part of broad access operation. "AI mainly improves established attacks by making them faster, more personalized, and easier to scale," Abnormal AI said. "Agentic intrusion chains and prompt injection are more distinct because they depend directly on deployed AI systems."

11rij62.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 31, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Attack The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added two security flaws impacting Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, following active exploitation in the wild. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-111357 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A missing authentication for a critical function vulnerability that could allow a local authenticated attacker to escalate their privileges. CVE-2026-118527 (CVSS score: 4.3) - A generation of predictable numbers or identifiers vulnerability that could allow a remote authenticated attacker to upload files with attacker-controlled content to a known location on disk. It's worth noting that the security bugs are part of an exploit chain that was first documented by Volexity earlier this month as weaponized in conjunction with an authentication bypass flaw (CVE-2026-104935, CVSS score: 8.6) by a previously undocumented threat actor dubbed UTA0576. CVE-2026-104935 was added to the KEV catalog on October 13, 2026. "This exploit chain combined an authentication bypass, a remote code execution (RCE), and a privilege escalation vulnerability to achieve unauthenticated root-level code execution," Volexity noted. Unlike other attacks that typically exploit such flaws to deploy web shells or malware, UTA0576 has been observed leveraging the flaws to extract credentials and limited Active Directory metadata; conduct host reconnaissance; and search for administrator passwords and BitLocker recovery keys. Ivanti said that, around the time the details were published, it was still working on developing fixes for the local privilege escalation (LPE) vulnerability exploited in the attack chain. Patches for both CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 are now available in the following versions of ICS - 25.1.1.2 and prior (Fixed in 25.1.1.3) 22.8R2.5 and prior (Fixed in 22.8R2.6) "At the time of discovery of exploitation, Ivanti had a fix developed for CVE-2026-104935 which was already in QA for supported versions, and we made the decision to not delay getting a fix to customers that resolved the primary exploitation path when the LPE was discovered," Ivanti explained. "Because of this, our focus was initially centered on the disclosure of CVE-2026-104935 and providing protection for our customers as quickly as possible." The company also noted that it discovered a portion of this vulnerability as part of its product security program and patched it in the July release 25.1.3.0, adding it had been working to backport the fix to other supported versions when exploitation activity occurred. The latest release addresses all vulnerabilities which were chained and exploited in the wild. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are required to apply the fixes for CVE-2026-111357 by November 2, 2026, and CVE-2026-118527 by November 13, 2026.

gukvs2.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 31, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security A malicious ChatGPT share link could run an attacker's code in the logged-in session of anyone who opened it, allowing them to read their private conversations, researchers at the security firm Parameter showed. The researchers reported the flaw through OpenAI's bug bounty program on October 18, and OpenAI fixed it eight days later and rated it P1, its most serious category. The trap was an ordinary ChatGPT conversation shared via its public link. It could be sent the same way as any real shared chat: by email, as a chat message, as a support ticket, or as a social post. The victim did not have to install anything, join a workspace, or sign in through the attacker. In the most reliable version of the attack, they opened the link and clicked ChatGPT's Preview button once. In a later version, Parameter set the page to open Preview on its own, so opening the link was the only step. What the Attacker Could Do Once the link opened, the attacker's code ran inside the victim's signed-in session with the same access as the real ChatGPT site. It listed the victim's recent conversations, opened a private chat that had never been shared with the attacker, and sent a small portion of it to a server controlled by the researchers. The code called ChatGPT's own signed-in APIs directly, rather than copying what happened to be on the screen. Because it ran with the victim's full web access, its reach was not limited to those chats. "Essentially, we could perform any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account," the researchers wrote. The work was a controlled test. Parameter does not report any real-world use of the flaw, and ran its private-chat proof between separate accounts rather than against real users. How the Link Broke Out of Its Sandbox Here is how the chain worked, according to Parameter. ChatGPT can turn a block of HTML in a chat into a small web page through a feature called Preview. Because that page can hold any code, ChatGPT runs it in a locked-down frame on a separate web address, where it cannot read the main ChatGPT page around it. That sandbox held. The way in came from a second feature in the same conversation. The shared chat also contained an interactive graph, and drawing it loaded a math library called MathLive into the main ChatGPT page. Loading MathLive left a listener running there that accepted messages about its on-screen keyboard. A message passed between browser frames is safe only if the receiver checks who sent it. Parameter found that this listener accepted a keyboard message from any sender, and that the message was allowed to carry raw HTML. The Preview could then reach across the boundary and hand attacker HTML to the trusted main page. That HTML built a new frame that the browser treated as part of chatgpt.com. A script loaded from YouTube then supplied the code that ran inside it. ChatGPT's content security policy limits where a page's scripts may come from. It blocked inline code but allowed scripts from YouTube, which is why that step worked. What OpenAI Fixed, and What Users Should Do Parameter said OpenAI reproduced both the code execution and the private-chat proof, raised the severity from P2 to P1, and rolled a fix across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. By October 26, both versions rejected the messages the attack relied on. The researchers traced the problem to three design choices that lined up: MathLive acted on a message that changed its settings without checking which frame had sent it. That message was allowed to carry raw HTML as keyboard-layout data. The HTML could create a frame that was not sandboxed and inherited the chatgpt.com identity. The YouTube step was only the final workaround, not the cause. Blocking it alone would still leave an untrusted Preview able to push HTML into the main site. ChatGPT users do not need to do anything. The fix is on OpenAI's side, with nothing to install or reset. Parameter published its writeup on October 28, after the fix. OpenAI paid a total of $5,000 for the report.

vvgq5d.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 31, 2026Threat Intelligence / Network Security Threat actors are launching about 8,226 network-layer distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks per hour, Cloudflare revealed Thursday. The web infrastructure and security company said it autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer (L3) DDoS attacks and 14.4 trillion HTTP DDoS requests in the third quarter of 2026. That amounts to 197,400 attacks per day, or one attack every 0.44 seconds. In comparison, a total of 13.2 million and 10.0 million L3 DDoS attacks were recorded in Q2 and Q1 2026, respectively. The increase has been linked to DDoS-for-hire booter or stresser services that are responsible for hundreds of thousands of attacks. "Short-burst, low-bandwidth attacks lasting under 10 minutes and 1 Gbps surged by 208%," the Cloudforce One threat intelligence team said in its quarterly DDoS Threat Report shared with The Hacker News. An interesting trend is the decline of hyper-volumetric attacks exceeding 1 Tbps by 69% from the previous quarter – going from 805 attacks in Q2 to 251 in Q3 – likely as a result of law enforcement actions against AISURU, KimWolf, JackSkid, and Mossad earlier this March. Still, the threat remains far from completely neutralized, given the emergence of new variants like Dysphoria and Evooo1Bot, Cloudflare warned. Another notable shift is the decline in Connectionless Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (CLDAP) floods, while DNS amplification jumped 215% to account for 3.43% of all network-layer attacks. The most targeted industries include media, production, and publishing; information technology and services; gambling and casinos; computer software; and telecommunications providers. The U.S., China, Indonesia, the U.K., and Türkiye emerged as the most attacked countries during the time period, with Canada and Israel entering the top 10 ranking, fueled by attacks targeting Canada's retail, telecommunications, and marketing sectors.

1vp329y.text: Chinese state-sponsored threat actors have been observed using a Go-based artificial intelligence (AI)-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX in attacks aimed at high-value targets simultaneously. The activity has been attributed by CrowdStrike to a China-based "targeted intrusion adversary" it tracks under the moniker Vapor Panda (previously VexatiousTemper). First identified in February 2021, the hacking group overlaps with a threat cluster detailed by Trend Micro as Earth Estries. "Agentic tooling like ARTEX enables this scale of expansion at speed, allowing a small team to pursue a wider target set than manual operations would support, rather than a wholesale shift away from the adversary's established access-development mission," CrowdStrike said in a Thursday analysis. Starting October 17, 2026, Vapor Panda is said to have used the AI tool against more than 200 distinct organizations across the world, including foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East; semiconductor, defense, and think tank organizations in the U.S.; and telecommunications providers in multiple regions. Some of the notable targets listed by CrowdStrike are listed below - Foreign ministries of two Latin America-based countries, Central America, and Asia A Middle East-based interior ministry A European country's foreign ministry, presidency, and prime minister's office, along with defense, justice, finance, and intelligence entities 19 U.S.-based organizations in the pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense, nuclear, and financial sectors Telecommunications providers in the U.S., Belgium, and the Philippines Post-exploitation activity has been confirmed at nine organizations, allowing the attacker to deploy BLOODALCHEMY, a derivative of ShadowPad, followed by credential spraying, network scanning, and reconnaissance. Vapor Panda is also said to have conducted password-spraying and credential-scanning activity against at least 12 additional organizations, including U.S.-based think tanks and government entities in Europe. Central to the operation is the use of ARTEX with DeepSeek and an as-yet-unknown, subscription-based commercial large language model (LLM) to conduct the intrusions at scale, leveraging an army of planner and worker agents that coordinate with each other in pursuit of a common goal to move from initial access to host reconnaissance and lateral movement. A human operator in the loop oversees the operation, directing the agents to write web shells, extract domain administrator passwords, and enumerate endpoint sensor coverage. "In a single intrusion, Vapor Panda's planning agents consumed on the order of 1.4 billion input tokens, indicating the scale of the automated activity and implying far higher consumption across the operation as a whole," CrowdStrike said. Unlike some campaigns that used to assist with individual digital break-ins, the use of ARTEX is at a much higher level to run multiple engagements concurrently, with the human operator only stepping in to steer the agents to accomplish their objective, while taking steps to bypass endpoint defenses. Analysis of the recovered transcripts highlights the use of ARTEX in combination with tried-and-tested approaches - Chaining an unsigned Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) assertion and an XML external entity (XXE) flaw to query the cloud Instance Metadata Service. This is followed by obtaining a role that can issue administration commands to thousands of instances before escalating access to recover an enterprise administrator account. Deploying web shells, abusing an unauthenticated orchestration service to obtain root access in a production container environment, reading Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) passwords, and leveraging resource-based constrained delegation to impersonate a privileged account. Supplying the agent with a set of authentication keys that had not been rotated since 2022, which then uses those keys to forge an administrator token and read mailboxes. In the next phase, the agent uses VPN configurations recovered from a user's sent mail, along with a VPN client key originating from a purported May 2024 email leak, to reach the internal network. "Across these engagements, the agents pursued multiple attack paths in parallel, spanning web applications, cloud services, container environments, Active Directory, and mail and VPN infrastructure," CrowdStrike explained. "They shifted to alternative approaches when a path failed. This breadth likely enables a single operator to apply a wider range of techniques against more targets at once than would be feasible through manual operations." The development comes as ARTEX has witnessed broad adoption among threat actors in a short span of time, prompting its developer Li Puhua ("Autumn-27") to take it closed source. "It orchestrates multiple LLM backends to autonomously perform reconnaissance, vulnerability identification, and exploitation, significantly lowering the technical barrier for conducting complex intrusion campaigns," Zscaler ThreatLabz said in a report published earlier this month. One of Many Panda Threat Clusters The disclosure also coincides with the emergence of four previously undocumented China-linked state-sponsored threat groups known as Hollow Panda, Overcast Panda, Titan Panda, and Veiled Panda, which have targeted a broad range of sectors across the world for intelligence gathering and intellectual property theft. Overcast Panda, described as "one of the most operationally sophisticated and persistent threats facing organizations with personnel traveling to China," has been linked to close access intrusions in which the adversary has deployed their proprietary FlowCloud backdoor on victims' devices via direct physical access when those targets were in the country. FlowCloud is launched by means of DLL sideloading, with its components designed to fly under the radar and resist forensic analysis. Command-and-control (C2) is accomplished through legitimate cloud infrastructure in an attempt to further conceal their presence. "FlowCloud itself is a sophisticated, purpose-built tool uniquely associated with Overcast Panda," CrowdStrike said. "Once deployed, FlowCloud provides the adversary with persistent, covert remote access to the target device, enabling keylogging, screen capture, file collection, and credential harvesting." Titan Panda, on the other hand, has been observed targeting legal billing software by exploiting a hard-coded Internet Information Services (IIS) machine key vulnerability in Intapp Time Server to achieve remote code execution across law firms. The attacks, first detected in April 2026, led to the deployment of an in-memory framework called IceGiant to carry out reconnaissance, persistence, lateral movement, and data exfiltration. The threat actor is assessed to be operational since at least 2021, compromising several legal organizations in North America for over two years. "How Titan Panda obtained the default machine keys is unknown, though IIS compromise of a legal entity running Intapp Time Server may have exposed the hardcoded keys in the application's configuration file, enabling ViewState deserialization attacks against any organization running default installations," CrowdStrike said.

flr5.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 30, 2026Vulnerability / Endpoint Security TeamViewer has fixed a flaw that lets the machine being controlled in a remote session attack the computer that connected to control it. In a TeamViewer session, the computer that connects and takes control is the viewer, and the machine it controls is the host. A malicious or compromised host can exploit the flaw to crash the viewer's TeamViewer and, depending on the platform, may also run code on the viewer's computer. This works only after the user starts a remote-control session to that host. The fix is in TeamViewer version 15.83. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-111585 and scored 8.8 out of 10, in the high range. It affects the TeamViewer Full Client on Windows, Linux, and macOS, the Windows Portable edition, and the Android Remote Control app, in all versions before 15.83. For this flaw, TeamViewer's bulletin lists the Full Client, Portable, and Android app, but not the Host. The same 15.83 update fixes two other flaws in that bulletin that do affect the Host, so people running the Host should update as well. Omri Dar, a researcher at security firm Remedio, published a technical account of the flaw on October 29. In this bug, he wrote, "the attacker is the host and the victim is the viewer." In a remote session, the host tells the viewer how large its screen image is. The viewer uses that size to set aside memory, but the calculation can overflow and reserve too little. Screen data that arrives afterward is then written past the end of that space. At a minimum, this crashes the viewer's TeamViewer session, and the host can trigger the crash again whenever they want. On Windows, Remedio says it took the bug further, bypassing the operating system's built-in exploit defenses and running code of its choosing in the viewer. The demonstration used a stand-in on the host to supply part of the attack data, so it is not yet an attack carried out entirely over the network. That result was shown only on Windows. Whether the same works on macOS, Linux, or Android is not covered in the write-up. TeamViewer only says that code execution is possible, depending on the platform. The attack needs no password and no extra click beyond accepting the session, and it works in TeamViewer's default setup, Dar wrote. The flaw affects all versions before 15.83, including 15.82, the security update TeamViewer released in September. Updating last month did not remove it. What to Do The only fix TeamViewer offers is to update, and it lists no workaround. Current users should move to 15.83 or later. The fixed builds for older supported branches are in the table above. The same 15.83 update also fixes two other high-severity flaws in the same bulletin, including a separate code-execution flaw affecting Linux and macOS. A companion bulletin the same day, TV-2026-1012, fixes six more flaws in TeamViewer's Remote Management add-ons, delivered by automatic update. TeamViewer said that when it published the fix, it was unaware of any attacks exploiting the flaw. The vulnerability is not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of its October 29 listing. Remedio reported no attacks in the wild and did not release exploit code.

1u3520n.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 30, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security Threat actors have been observed attempting to exploit a high-severity security flaw in WordPress Core shortly after patches were released. The vulnerability, which does not have a CVE identifier, relates to a case of remote code execution impacting WordPress Core versions 4.7 through 7.1.3. It carries a CVSS score of 8.1 on the CVSS scoring system. Patches for the flaw were released on October 28, 2026. "This is due to predictable, web-accessible staging paths used during full-package core upgrades," Wordfence said. "This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to execute code on the server during the upgrade window." The WordPress security company noted that successful exploitation requires an "attacker to hit a very narrow window while WordPress is unpacking a complete Core update." The issue boils down to the fact that affected versions unpack new files part of a full-package Core update into a predictable directory under "wp-content/upgrade." This copy also includes the WordPress installer. "Because the staging directory is web-accessible on many servers, an unauthenticated attacker who requests the installer at precisely the right moment can interact with the staged WordPress copy and progress to PHP code execution," Alex Thomas, who leads the Wordfence Threat Response Team, said. A threat actor who is able to win the race condition can gain the ability to execute code on the server, assuming the following conditions are met - A full-package update containing the installer files Public web and PHP access to the staging tree A predictable or discovered staging path, and Adequate time to complete the attack before WordPress cleans up the temporary files Although that window has been observed to last only seconds in normal lab environments, threat actors are polling vulnerable paths, such as "setup-config.php," repeatedly in an attempt to trigger the flaw. Over the past 24 hours, Wordfence said it has blocked 62,969 attacks targeting the vulnerability. "Two of the largest sources repeatedly polled small groups of sites for roughly 14.5 hours, behavior consistent with trying to catch the brief upgrade window," Thomas said. "Other sources tested many staging-directory and version-name variations." "Not every request used the exact vulnerable path, but the sustained polling and exact-layout probes show that attackers quickly understood the race condition and began targeting it." With active exploitation attempts already underway, WordPress site owners are advised to update to version 7.1.4 as soon as possible and look for suspicious requests to PHP files located under "wp-content/upgrade," as well as unfamiliar administrator accounts, plugins, or PHP files.

d2s85l.text: A public proof of concept has exposed a flaw in Telegram Desktop that could let attackers steal local files and take over accounts after a user clicks a crafted external link. Tracked as CVE-2026-107181, the vulnerability affects versions before 7.2.9 and carries a CVSS 4.0 severity rating of 8.6 (High). Researcher Beaksec published the technical write-up on October 3, 2026, and updated it on October 7. VulnCheck assigned the CVE that day. The reported attack reaches Telegram’s local session data, making account takeover possible when the victim has not enabled a local passcode. The weakness lies in how Telegram Desktop handles links opened outside the app. When Telegram is already running, another instance passes the link to it through a local communication channel, known as inter-process communication, or IPC. That channel failed to escape a character used to separate records. An attacker could place the character inside a crafted link and make Telegram read part of the link as another command. The CVE record classifies this as CWE-143, improper handling of record delimiters. PoC Released for Telegram Desktop Flaw According to ThreatWire’s research, the injected command could access an outdated internal helper designed for release publishing. The helper could read local files and send them to a chat without permission checks or user confirmation. The result is file theft through Telegram itself. Stolen session files could let an attacker reuse the victim’s logged-in account. Earlier reporting on Telegram account hijacking through voicemail shows another route to account loss, but that method is separate from this Desktop vulnerability. The researcher demonstrated the chain on Windows using Telegram Desktop 6.9.3 and reported that it remained present through 7.2.8. Although the CVE covers Telegram Desktop generally, the write-up does not demonstrate the attack on macOS or Linux. The link must be opened outside Telegram, such as from a browser. Links clicked inside Telegram follow a different processing path and are not affected. A browser may also ask for permission before launching the desktop app. The demonstrated chain depends on automatic group file downloads and settings that allow anyone to add the victim to a group. These conditions matter when judging the “one-click” claim. Previous EvilVideo coverage also highlighted download settings, although that issue affected Telegram for Android rather than Desktop. Telegram fixed the issue in commit db3405699f on September 16 and released version 7.2.9 on September 17. The reported changes remove the legacy helper, escape the record separator, and strengthen handling of mixed record types. The release notes mention only a rendering fix, not the security issue. No vendor security advisory is identified in the supplied reporting. The CVSS 3.1 score is 8.1, while CVSS 4.0 gives 8.6. Both ratings describe the same flaw. Users should update every Telegram Desktop installation to 7.2.9 or later. Until then, restrict group invitations, stop automatic downloads, and enable a local passcode. Treat unexpected browser prompts to open Telegram cautiously. As of October 9, the supplied reporting identifies no known exploitation or CISA KEV listing. A public PoC demonstrates feasibility, not confirmed attacks. The public write-up should not be mistaken for independent attack confirmation. Users who suspect exposure should end other active sessions and review chats for unexpected file uploads. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. oapp2e.text: Anthropic has introduced OSS Scanner, a free service that checks critical open-source repositories for security vulnerabilities and sends findings directly to project maintainers. The opt-in program uses the company’s strongest AI models to run repeated scans, giving developers a faster route to potential flaws without waiting for human review. According to Anthropic’s service overview, OSS Scanner builds on its work with Project Glasswing. The company says it had reviewed more than 6,000 vulnerability reports by October 2026 through its existing disclosure process. The new service offers a separate path for projects willing to assess AI-generated reports. Anthropic OSS Scanner According to the GitHub repository, the scanner first builds an enrolled project inside an isolated virtual machine with network access enabled. This stage installs dependencies and prepares the software for testing. Anthropic then removes Internet access before the security audit begins, allowing scanning agents to examine the project within a restricted environment. Reports arrive by email with steps to reproduce the suspected issue and a proposed patch where available. Anthropic says its pipeline includes agents that double-check bugs and examine their root causes. However, these checks are automated. A human does not review the findings before maintainers receive them. After the first scan, the service checks projects again for newly introduced vulnerabilities and issues missed earlier. Scan frequency depends on factors such as demand and project usage. This extends Anthropic’s wider push into security research, including earlier work in which Claude uncovered 22 Firefox vulnerabilities. Core maintainers apply through the official GitHub repository by opening a pull request that adds a directory under projects/<name>. Each submission needs a project.yaml configuration containing the repository address and a primary contact email. Anthropic manually checks that applicants are core maintainers before accepting a project. Eligibility focuses on established projects with broad use, exposure to remote attacks, and significant infrastructure security impact. A Dockerfile must explain how to install dependencies and build the software. Developers can keep it in their own repository or beside project.yaml in the enrollment repository. Everything needed for building and testing must be downloaded during setup because the later audit cannot access the Internet. An optional threat_model.md file helps guide the scan. Maintainers can describe where untrusted input enters, which components are outside scope, and how they rate severity. They can also explain preferred report formats and patch requirements, reducing the need for the scanner to guess project-specific security expectations. Before applying, developers can use tools/validate.py to check their configuration and tools/check <name> to test the build. The checking tool runs with network access, so Anthropic warns users to test only trusted projects or use a separate machine. Configuration email addresses are public, making a dedicated security alias useful. Maintainers can add an OpenPGP public key for encrypted reports, but encrypted messages go only to the primary contact and cannot include additional recipients. Anthropic does not impose a 90-day disclosure deadline on unvalidated findings. However, a report later confirmed through its human-reviewed program may enter that disclosure process. This safeguard matters amid concerns about AI-generated vulnerability reports wasting maintainers’ time. Project owners still need to reproduce suspected flaws and test suggested fixes before treating them as confirmed vulnerabilities. Reports can be paused with disabled: true, while deleting the enrollment directory withdraws the project entirely Cut every SOC alert investigation by 21 min. 1u9k9io.text: Let’s Encrypt will cut its default TLS certificate lifetime from 90 days to 64 days on February 10, 2027, giving website operators less time between renewals. The change applies to certificates issued or renewed from that date, while subscribers can still choose shorter certificate profiles offering 45 days or roughly six days. Let’s Encrypt Certificate Lifetime According to the October 7 announcement published by Let’s Encrypt, the nonprofit certificate authority confirmed the schedule. Existing certificates will remain valid until their normal expiry dates, and Let’s Encrypt will not revoke them as part of the transition. It expects the final 90-day certificate to expire on May 11, 2027. The shorter lifetime limits how long a certificate can remain trusted after a private key is stolen or a certificate is issued incorrectly. It also makes reliable renewal systems more important, especially for teams still using fixed schedules or manual steps. The move is part of the wider shift toward shorter public TLS certificate lifetimes. Cybersecurity News previously covered the CA/Browser Forum’s plan to reduce maximum validity to 47 days. Let’s Encrypt is moving faster, with its default profile set to 45 days on February 16, 2028, as outlined in its earlier certificate lifetime roadmap. Let’s Encrypt will start issuing 64-day certificates in its staging environment on October 14, 2026. Administrators can use this test service to check renewal behavior before the production change. Staging certificates are not trusted by browsers and should not replace certificates on live websites. For automated setups, the key feature is ACME Renewal Information, or ARI. ACME is the protocol used to request and renew certificates automatically. ARI lets Let’s Encrypt tell a supported client when to renew, helping it adjust to shorter lifetimes without relying on a fixed calendar. Administrators should check their client’s documentation to confirm ARI support. When ARI isn’t available, Let’s Encrypt recommends renewing at about two-thirds of the certificate’s lifetime. For a 64-day certificate, that means around day 43, rather than waiting until the old 60-day renewal point. The authority also recommends searching cron jobs, wrapper scripts, and runbooks for hardcoded values such as 83, 80, or 60. These numbers may reveal renewal rules designed around 90-day certificates. Updating those rules now also prepares systems for the 45-day default planned for 2028. Alongside certificate validity, Let’s Encrypt will reduce authorization reuse from 30 days to 10 days. This is the period during which an earlier domain control check can support another certificate request without repeating that check. The reuse period will fall to seven hours in 2028. Let’s Encrypt says this supports upcoming validation rules and removes the need for separate Certificate Authority Authorization rechecks on older validation data. Most subscribers will not need changes unless their ACME setup specifically depends on authorization reuse. Rate limits will not change because of the shorter lifetimes, according to Let’s Encrypt’s rate limit guidance. ACME endpoints and certificate issuance chains will also remain unchanged. Operators should test the full certificate workflow, including deployment and service reloads, rather than checking renewal alone. Teams managing many websites should also confirm that renewed certificates reach every server and that monitoring checks the certificate actually served to users after each reload. Alerts for failed renewals can help teams catch problems before expiry. The practical priority is dependable automation that keeps certificates current as renewal windows shrink.
